Mr. Speaker, over the week end I read in the newspapers that the first live rat had appeared in the province of Alberta. That is a fact

I am not joking about it, and we understand the menace. Strangely enough, it came from the east, and was found in the city of Edmonton. VETERANS AFFAIRS

speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
maintopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to table copies in English and in French of a regulation made under the Department of Veterans Affairs Act by order in council P.C. 1266 of March 10, 1950.
This regulation permits this department to give hospitalization and treatment to veterans who are ineligible under present regulations, but who are covered as to hospital costs by private or provincial government insurance plans; or who, though not insured, have the means to pay for the treatment for which they may apply at D.V.A. hospitals.
The prime responsibility of the hospitals maintained by the Department of Veterans Affairs is to treat those who have pensionable disabilities, and such veterans will continue to have an absolute priority in rights to beds in our hospitals. Treatment under the new regulation will be given to paying veteran patients only to the extent that beds are not required for entitled veterans.
It is the intention to try out these new arrangements for the period of a year, during which their value will be assessed and the appropriate regular scale of rates for the various districts of Canada worked out.
For the immediate future the number of beds available for this purpose will not be great, so that no assurance is given that accommodation will be available for all who apply.
Fuller details on the plan will be available after March 31 next at D.V.A. district offices and through veterans organizations.

maintopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS

As to his first question, an attempt is being made to work into the plan those benefits accruing in British Columbia and Saskatchewan under their provincial insurance plans.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. McCann (Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys; Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week a number of questions were asked in reference to order in council P.C. 458, having to do with depreciation. The one of which I received notice was asked by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), and was as follows, as reported at page 562 of Hansard:
In view of the fact that this order in council was made effective for 1949 taxation and may cause confusion among farmers who, in accordance with the law, filed their interim returns on December 31, will the minister consider delaying its coming into effect for this year?
That, together with other questions, prompted me to say that I would make a short statement on the matter, which I propose to do now.
Under the Income War Tax Act, which applied to 1948 and prior years, no depreciation was allowable except what the Minister of National Revenue, in his sole discretion, approved. The Income Tax Act, which applies to 1949 and subsequent years, provides that allowances in respect of capital costs will be as prescribed by regulation of the governor in council. If the regulation is suspended, the taxpayer will be deprived of his right to make any deduction for depreciation for 1949. It is for that reason I quoted the request for the suspension of the order in council.
Important changes were introduced in the 1949 budget, and, at the request of some members of parliament, the government agreed to amend the law so that certain provisions would not apply to farmers and fishermen. These were specifically the new method of computing depreciation, and the recapture provisions. As soon as possible after parliament approved the legislation, regulations were prepared, approved by the governor in council, and published. The rates applicable to farmers and fishermen are clearly set out therein. These rates have been made uniform with the rates available to all other taxpayers in Canada, having regard to the fact that farmers and fishermen are excluded from certain provisions of the law as mentioned above. For example, the fifteen per cent rate, allowed to farmers and fishermen on the straight-line basis on automotive equipment, results in an asset being depreciated by ninety per cent in six years. The thirty per cent rate, on the reducing-balance basis on automotive equipment, applicable to all taxpayers other than farmers and fishermen, results in an asset being depreciated by 88 -24 per cent in six years.


The comparison, therefore, is rather in favour of the farmer, as I indicated when I was making my reply.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT
speechtext:
The Canadian representatives at the conference have been instructed to favour the accession of Germany and Japan to the agreement. I might say that there is some opposition to their accession, but Canada is favouring it.

be added to the agreement, a quantity which will permit Canada to have its allotment revised upward to the 230 million bushels that was originally thought to be our fair share of the world markets. The Address-Mr. Mayhew SPEECH FROM THE THRONE

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext: The house resumed, from Thursday, March 9, consideration of the motion of Mr. F. H. Larson for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Drew, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Coldwell.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. W. Mayhew (Minister of Fisheries):
maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) when earlier he was making his first report on the Colombo conference intimated that I would take part in this debate. My remarks will be divided into four main sections: the first concerning the international labour organization convention which was held at Mysore; the second with reference to the commonwealth conference in Colombo; the third, a reference to our own position, economically, in those countries; and the fourth, my own observations or speculations as to what we might do.
I want to assure you, sir, that at this time I am speaking entirely on my own behalf. Before proceeding with what I wish particularly to say, I wish to pay the usual well-earned tributes to the mover (Mr. Larson) and the seconder (Mr. Dumas) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, but I shall do it in a slightly different way. I think they have had an opportunity of becoming a little better known in the country as a whole. It is a great encouragement to us in this house to hear the younger men when they come in and make their maiden speeches. I think it is also a great encouragement to the people outside of this house to realize that there is a constant inflow of younger men who are capable, well-trained and prepared to fill vacancies as they occur in the ranks of the government of Canada. The fact that these young men have the urge, the spirit and the courage to go ahead with this career is, I think, one of the reasons why we should have so much confidence in our democratic system.
I should like also to say how grateful I am to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and to the Secretary of State for External Affairs for making it possible for Mrs. Mayhew and myself to take this extended trip, which has been interesting and beneficial to us. It is my hope, and I am sure it is that of Mrs. Mayhew, that the country will receive great benefit also, and in the same proportion; but I doubt whether that will be so.
I intend to speak about the meeting of the international labour organization, attendance at which was my chief mission while abroad, because I feel that the ILO is doing most

The Address-Mr. Mayhew valuable work and should be supported. The ILO is one of the oldest and most successful of all international organizations. It was established after the first world war as an agency of the league of nations; and it is the only part of the league that survived the second world war. It has increased its membership and expanded its activities considerably during the past few years, a fact which affords ample proof of its vitality and the support it is receiving. There are now more than sixty member countries represented in this organization.
The purpose of the international labour organization is to promote social justice in all countries. It seeks to do this by improving industrial relations, raising living standards, and helping to bring about economic and social stability through legislative action and international agreement. It is a unique organization in that it is tripartite; its members represent governments, employers and workers. This I believe is the secret of its strength. The ILO delegates appreciate the view of others and try to bring about harmony out of diversity. The ILO meetings are unique also in that, so far at least, they have been fairly free of the ideological and political differences which have so hampered the work of the United Nations.
The governing body of the international labour organization meets four times a year. It was the 110th meeting of the governing body which I attended in Mysore, India, late in December and early in January. This was a significant and important meeting, because it was the first in the thirty years' history of the ILO that has been held in Asia. It signified the increasing interest which Europe and the Americas are showing in this part of the world, and it was a tribute to the new and independent nations which have come into being. By holding this meeting in India the ILO gave proof of its desire to fulfil its obligations to all regions and to live up to the principles of universality.
This meeting in India achieved the useful purpose of focusing attention on the many and difficult labour and social problems in Asia. It brought t'o light the urgent need of these countries for financial and-chiefly- technological assistance. It also revealed the serious consequences which might result were such aid not forthcoming. I think that all the delegates became acutely aware of the fact that they could not, in their own interest, ignore the many problems of Asia. Social and economic improvement and higher standards of living cannot be obtained for one-half of the world while the other half is left to struggle for existence.
During intervals between meetings and on week ends I had the opportunity of travelling 
by car some four hundred miles around southern India. Mysore itself is somewhat off the beaten track; hence what we saw there, though typical of country life in India, is not' what will be found described in visitors' handbooks. We saw much that was beautiful, and we saw much of the potential wealth of that fascinating country.
Hon. members may be interested in the agenda of the governing body meeting; it will give an idea of the scope of the work of the organization. Perhaps I might then conclude this brief report by commenting on one or two of the more important items which were discussed.
I will not name all the items on the agenda, but only some in order to indicate the type of work they were doing: Proposals concerning fellowships; questions relating to freedom of association; report on action against unemployment; safety in coal mines; labour statistics; report of committee on salaried employees and professional workers; report of committee on recreation; report of committee on juvenile employment; report of officers of committee on social security experts; report of the technical assistance committee; proposed establishment of an Asian advisory committee.
These are some of the twenty-six items on the agenda of the session.
One of the more interesting proposals was that concerning fellowships. The governing body agreed to establish a fellowship scheme under which young men and women, chiefly from underdeveloped countries, could obtain practical training in countries technologically more advanced. This scheme would supplement a similar but larger fellowship scheme already in operation under the United Nations. By adopting this proposal the international labour organization recognized the need for technical assistance in backward countries.
Another important item on the agenda was social security. In the early years after the first world war the ILO drafted conventions and recommendations on standards of social security, and these became the models upon which many countries based their national legislation. Now the organization is planning to review these conventions and recommendations, to integrate them and make them more practicable in view of the advances that have been made in recent times. It has instructed a special committee of experts to revise these international instruments and set forth the objectives and minimum standards of an integrated, fully-rounded program.
The most difficult and contentious, and certainly the most important, subject discussed at the 110th session of the governing body

was the proposal that the ILO set up an international fact-finding and conciliation commission to investigate violation of trade union rights or freedom of association, alleged to exist in member countries. Canada, of course, supported the proposal, because nationally as well as internationally we are interested in maintaining union rights as well as union responsibilities.
The proposal approved by the governing body envisages the establishment of an international commission to investigate all bona fide charges alleging the violation of trade union rights. It would consist of nine members, all of whom would be respected and recognized authorities in labour matters. Complaints referred to them would first be examined by the governing body who would weed out all frivolous charges, and only legitimate grievances would be investigated by the commission.
As the request of the government concerned is required before action can be taken by the commission, it remains to be seen just how far Russia and her satellite countries will go in permitting investigation of conditions within their territories by an international body.
In concluding this report on the ILO meeting, I would like to say how much impressed I was by the manner in which this international labour organization operates. I am proud of the fact that Canada has been a member of it since its inception and is now rated as one of the eight nations of chief industrial importance. We have always had close ties with the ILO, having been host to its secretariat during the war. I hope that Canada will continue to participate as fully as possible in the work of this organization.
A detailed report has been forwarded to the Minister of Labour and is available for reference if anyone wishes any further information regarding it.
After the meeting of the international labour organization at Mysore, to which I have already referred as being somewhat off the beaten path, an opportunity was given to us of seeing some of the village life of India. We left our plane on the first part of our journey to Bangalore. It was some ninety miles into Mysore, and in that stretch of ninety miles we passed one Indian village after another. We spent ten days in Mysore, and drove back to Bangalore. There we took a plane to Madras and from Madras to Colombo. At Colombo we joined my colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs at the conference of ministers of external affairs.
I was very much pleased to have the opportunity of attending this conference and of
The Address-Mr. Mayhew meeting men whom we read about but rarely have a chance to see. To me-and I am off the regular path now-the chief good of the conference was not so much the deliberations of the meetings as the discussions at the functions, by way of various entertainment, and so on, that were held there and in Mysore; the opportunity it gave to each of the delegates to sit beside his neighbour at luncheons and other gatherings and to have informal talks. You can depend upon it that the good will that was generated in this conference was well worth while.
I would not like to have the house or the country think that we were a group of peregrinating individuals going round the world on a magic carpet, with a special magic eye pointed down to the oases and comforts and hospitality, and that only in those places did we try to do a job. Whether it was a magic eye or not, our trip was well planned. We met nothing but friendliness and the most cordial hospitality. I hope that some of my words-at least some of the earnestness that I try to express-will go back to the countries that received us and gave us such a wonderful time and the opportunity of seeing and knowing them.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: While the minister is thinking about Colombo and the places at which he was entertained at different times, perhaps he will say a word of encouragement to the natives and the people of Colombo with regard to their standard of living as compared with our own, and indicate that the Canadian people would be ready to help them out.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I hope that nothing that 1 have said or will say will in any way be considered as disparaging of these people. Indeed it is the very opposite. I could readily be quite optimistic if I were asked to live in that country. They have every reason to be hopeful for the future, and I would be the last to bring back a message of despair about India, Pakistan, Ceylon or the other countries that we had a chance to visit.
We hear a good many people speak of the magnitude of the task connected with bringing a better standard of living to these splendid and hard-working people. They are as kind as any other people in the world, and they are anxious to do better. To hon. members who are interested I would recommend a reading of an article by Edwin Muller in the March issue of the Reader's Digest, entitled "A way to lessen world hunger". There you will get some idea as to what could be done without spending a vast amount of money.
It must be remembered that India and Ceylon, as well as all of south Asia, are not one-crop countries. They have no difficulty,

The Address-Mr. Mayhew if they have water, in getting three, four, and in some places five crops a year. It must also be remembered that that part of the world is very backward in the matter of tools. In a sense they are the victims of the kind of thing that we are victims of in Canada; they are as much afraid of the modern tool displacing workers as we are afraid of immigration. Both will bring prosperity-in India, the advanced tool, and in Canada, immigration.
Anyone in the United States or Canada who would think of employing a tractor, a large combine or a heavy plow would have in mind something which is not known over there and which would not do the job. The agricultural areas are divided into plots of three, four or five acres. Plots of these sizes are about all one family could cultivate properly if it is to take off three or four crops in the year.
Perhaps I should tell the house, however, what we did see. In watering the land-and what I am about to say is more particularly true of Egypt-they dip the water with buckets which carry it to the top of the bank, at which point it is poured into a sluice to irrigate the land. A treadmill may be used to pump the water. Others use the ancient method of the Archimedean screw, the principle of which I am sure is familiar to all hon. members. In that process a man turns a crank and a small volume of water comes up. A farm pump, with which we are familiar in Canada, would probably irrigate twenty times as much land as the methods they are now using.
It will be seen from what I am saying that the problem is neither colossal nor spectacular. On the contrary it could be handled in a simple fashion. These people should be encouraged to see whether the modern equipment we have been using could be used to their advantage. These are new countries with a new lease on life and new leaders. They are driving ahead at a rate which commands the admiration of all and requires very little encouragement. As they make progress they will have more rubber, more tea, more coffee, more spices

more of all the things which are needed in this country and which will be available there in greater quantities when they really get going. I look forward with confidence to the possibilities of these countries reaching a high level of production in quick time.
I fear I am completely off the track so far as what I had intended to say is concerned. I shall not take up too much time in saying some of the things I had intended to say, and which are set out in my notes, in the careful preparation of which I received some help but which because of the shortage of time I cannot complete.

One point I should like to make which, it seems to me, has been overlooked in the debate thus far. There seemed to be a feeling that all that took place at Colombo was a conference of foreign ministers, and that the discussions were all political. That, of course, is not so. Concurrently with those discussions were others concerning trade and commerce and finance. From Canada there were three representatives who attended and who worked continually while the other conference was in progress.
At the conclusion of the Colombo conference we left for Karachi, at which point we spent two days with the people in that capital city of Pakistan. We did not see much of Pakistan outside the capital, but I can say that in Karachi we saw in progress the building of a new capital which in a few years' time will be well worthy of that fine country. While there, however, we did have an opportunity to talk about trade with practically all the ministers. Perhaps in my conversations I was in a position to speak with greater freedom than was my colleague, and to take greater advantage of the time to speak about trade, not forgetting, of course, sales of fish.
I believe that in those conferences we had considerable success. I have before me some trade figures in which hon. members may be interested. They disclose that as to Ceylon, Pakistan and India, only Ceylon has a favourable balance of trade with Canada, and the amount is fairly substantial. In 1949 Canada exported to Ceylon approximately $2,159,000 worth of goods, the important commodities being milk products, railway ties and newsprint. In the same period we imported $11,635,000 worth of goods, of which tea accounted for $8,765,000 and rubber $1,593,000.
Our exports to Pakistan in 1949 amounted to approximately $18,097,000, in which was included over $2 million worth of commercial vehicles and more than $8 million worth of defence stores, plus another $1 million for ships and aircraft. During the same period we imported about $1,193,000 worth of goods, consisting mainly of jute and tea.
Canada's exports to India in 1949 were valued at approximately $72,551,000, of which $22,960,000 was for wheat and flour, and $27,125,000 for locomotives and parts. Other important commodities included newsprint, railway rails and track materials, commercial vehicles, railway cars, non-ferrous metals, fertilizers, aluminum and ships. Our imports in the same period amounted to $26,233,000 including $8,555,000 worth of tea, $10,528,000 worth of jute fabrics, $1,564,000 worth of nuts, and $1,270,000 worth of carpets.
Leaving India, we had a brief stay in Singapore. Here, despite political unrest in the northern part of the Malayan federation and

Indonesia which could affect the flow of rubber and tin, government officials and businessmen interviewed did not appear apprehensive, but on the contrary were optimistic.
In 1949 Canada exported to Singapore approximately $5,439,000 worth of goods, of which $1,741,000 was for milk products; $800,000 was for commercial vehicles and parts; over $400,000 was for wheat flour, and about $450,000 for newsprint. In the same period we imported goods valued in excess of $16,208,000 from the same area, the main items being rubber to a value of $10,139,000, and tin to a value of $4,834,000.
Our next stop was probably our most spectacular, to the extent that our plane, having been adroitly navigated, despite low-hanging clouds, through a mountain-studded approach to the airstrip, decided to blow two tires just after we touched down in Hong Kong. No two blowouts ever received as much attention as they did.
Here again we found a spirit of confidence and evidence of considerable current development. The dislocation in the trade with China is, however, making itself felt, and stores and warehouses are stacked with merchandise destined for China when trading facilities are restored.
Last year Canada exported to Hong Kong goods valued at approximately $10 million, including $3,438,000 worth of wheat flour, over $840,000 worth of fountain pens, and $490,000 worth of newsprint, plus quantities of fish, milk products and fertilizer. We imported from Hong Kong during the same period goods worth $2,989,000, including approximately $810,000 worth of tin, $230,000 worth of peanuts, and $185,000 worth of fireworks.
Our final trade talks were held in Tokyo with General Mac Arthur and members of his staff, and with Japanese ministers, officials and businessmen. External trade policy was placed in the hands of the Japanese authorities only as of the first of this year. Nevertheless we were satisfied that Japan was anxious to spend just as many dollars in Canada as we spent in that country, and that in any case there was no tendency to discriminate against Canada in favour of other hard currency countries.
In 1949 we exported to Japan goods valued at nearly $5,860,000, including $2,145,000 worth of pulp, some $818,000 worth of whisky, and quantities of beef, newsprint, nickel and sulphur. Our imports from Japan last year amounted to $5,551,000, including toys, approximately $950,000; textiles and products, approximately $1,350,000; oranges, approximately $493,000; and small quantities of porcelain, pottery and tea.
The Address-Mr. Mayhew
In my opinion a peace treaty should be negotiated with Japan at an early day. Until that is done and Japan is able to see her way through the clouds, I do not know exactly what is going to happen. She has lost her colonies; only 20 per cent of her land is arable; her population is increasing, and all she has to sell is what can be produced with her own hands. Neither we nor the United States are any too anxious to take in the products she makes, because we fear it will put our own people out of employment. We must take a realistic view of the position, but I do not think anyone can measure what will happen to Japan until after a peace treaty has been negotiated.
I hope I am not interfering with the affairs of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), but I do want to indicate one plan which may or may not have merit. I do not think any plan can be offered that would not entail a considerable amount of speculation and meet with great difficulties.
Our export position has been unique. Generally we have developed sufficient balances with overseas countries to pay for our dollar deficit with the United States. In the past this overseas trade has been regarded more as a financial operation than as a disposal of exports. Essentially this problem remains, although it has greatly changed its character in the past few years. Our dollar deficit with the United States is gradually contracting, and our industries have made many readjustments in the last four years to the new international trade position.
The fact remains, however, that these overseas markets remain essential for certain raw materials-wheat, flour, tobacco, fish, cheese, eggs and bacon, and certain manufactures, such as automotive goods, textiles, rubber, machinery, and chemicals. In relation to primary commodities, overseas restrictions will produce export surpluses for us; in relation to manufactured commodities, the market restrictions will show themselves in unemployment. The federal government will be pressed to take different kinds of action to meet these problems, but in effect the problems will be identical and similar in origin, and will best be met by action that expands our overseas business. Our need, therefore, is to find means of disposing of export surpluses to the non-dollar areas and of finding acceptable imports from these countries. It is clear that a solution cannot be found by attaching ourselves to the dollar or the sterling currency areas. The problem is not a financial one, but one of the exchange of commodities. So far as Canada goes, the problem is perhaps unique, and a unique solution has to be found. In short, Canada has to find a middle way.

The Address-Mr. May hew
Because of our previous rather elementary trade mechanism we lack many of the facilities necessary for meeting problems of this kind. We lack the knowledge to be found in many of the European brokerage and merchant houses, the shipping knowledge, etc. The sterling area has these facilities within it and uses them in handling the European and oriental trades. Because of this, our exporters lack direct contact with many markets that might want our goods and that might in return supply us with imports. Many countries may not be earning all the dollars they can in sales or in potential production. Individual Canadian firms that look for barter arrangements often find themselves faced with a sale of commodities in which they have no interest. Many of these difficulties may be overcome by extending the scope of barter arrangements for the particular commodities we have in surplus.
As the idea of the joint stock company developed originally to handle foreign trade in days when international financing was impossible, perhaps it can now be extended. Instead of using the concept only on a company basis, it might be extended to an inter-company basis. We might consider, therefore, the establishment of a national export-import corporation, beginning its use with countries that now take few Canadian goods. We should recognize that this may be more possible in Canada than in almost any other country, because so large a part of our trade now is concentrated in only a few firms. Likewise, large parts of the primary surpluses may soon be owned by government.
It seems possible, therefore, to work out in Canada a combination between the very large groups of manufacturers and wholesalers, to provide both the management and the finance to operate bilateral deals and to overcome the lack of facilities that faces any single corporation. The government, through the corps of trade commissioners, could furnish valuable assistance. Such a body could barter parcels of mixed Canadian merchandise for mixed imports from the non-dollar countries, and such merchandise could of course include capital equipment as well as foodstuffs or raw material.
This instrument might be used experimentally as an additional. means of meeting the surplus-unemployment problems. If the subject is not approached in some such way, there is a danger that the various boards handling surpluses will operate independently on a give-away basis, and that the various local unemployment problems will also be tackled by relief, public works or other means that will alleviate but not remove the basic difficulty.

This last part is purely my own, but it is the result of thinking while away and after coming home. We have to find some way out of this difficulty. If anyone knows of a better way, it is up to him to tell us. I assure the house that I am not speaking in any way for the government in offering this plan. I imagine it is new to the government.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I want first to congratulate the mover (Mr. Larson) and the seconder (Mr. Dumas) of the address in reply to the speech from the-throne on the splendid job they did, considering the material that was placed at their disposal. I should like also to congratulate the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Harris) on his appointment as minister of the new Department of Citizenship and Immigration.
In speaking at this time I am aware that much of what I have to say may be repetition, but I have no apology to offer in view of what was done last Wednesday by the right hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). It was bad enough to have to read the press report of the speech he made on May 28, 1949. To have to sit and listen to a repetition of it here was only adding insult to injury, and I am sure many farmers across this country will agree with that statement. What the minister hoped to prove is beyond my comprehension, unless it was to show- and I am sure it was not necessary to have further proof

that he is one of the smartest politicians, with a capital "P", that Canada has ever seen.
The low price program to which Canadian farmers submitted during the war years to my knowledge was without parallel anywhere in the world, and simple justice demands that their sacrifice be rewarded by the fulfilment of the government's pledge to provide a measure of stability in the post-war years, when economic readjustments might threaten to undermine farming. Here I should like to quote from a speech delivered by the former leader of the Liberal party, Mr. King, in a national broadcast on December 4, 1943:
I wish tonight to thank the farmers of Canada for their magnificent contribution to the battle of production. I wish as well to appeal to them to continue to help hold the front line against inflation by continuing to support the price ceiling. If, to help win the war, the farmers are asked to accept a ceiling on prices, we believe they are entitled to a floor under prices to ensure them against an agricultural depression after the war. As an essential part of its post-war policy the government intends to ask parliament, at the next session, to place a floor under the prices of the main farm commodities.
In 1944, therefore, the Agricultural Prices Support Act was passed, with the unanimous approval of all members of the House of Commons. Section 9 (2) of that act reads:

in prescribing prices under paragraphs (a) and (c) of subsection one of this section, the board shall endeavour to ensure adequate and stable returns for agriculture by promoting orderly adjustment from war to peace conditions and shall endeavour to secure a fair relationship between the returns from agriculture and those from other occupations.
As most hon. members will realize, this was the Progressive Conservative policy formulated under our previous leader, John Bracken, and forced upon this government by pressure from our party and from farm organizations across the country.

Very well, Mr. Speaker. Last fall, however, the intention of the government was made clear in a resolution placed on the order paper by the Minister of Agriculture, as follows:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide that section nine of the Agricultural Prices Support Act, 1944, shall continue in force for such period or periods as the governor in council may from time to time fix by proclamation, but shall expire upon the dissolution of the twenty-first parliament.
Since that is the only portion of the act that is workable as far as floor prices are concerned, I should say that resolution indicated the intention of this government to do away with that legislation.
By special efforts during the war Canadian farmers brought bacon exports up to a peak of 675 million pouhds during the thirteen months ending December 31, 1943. By 1947 our exports had fallen to 225 million pounds, and in 1949 a contract for 160 million pounds was signed, with the quantity sent to Great Britain only a little more than half that amount. It was never expected that we
The Address-Mr. Charlton could retain peak wartime bacon exports, but there was every reason to believe that a part of that market could and would be maintained. I want to quote the words of the Minister of Agriculture as they appear in Hansard for September 24, 1945, at pages 408 and 409: ... I wish to call attention to the contracts with Britain, because, after all, those contracts have established the floors right from the beginning of the war down to the present time.
And further:
If we in the dominion of Canada can produce 450 million pounds of bacon a year over and above what we require in this country, for the years that are ahead of us we shall just about be able to supply that part of the British market which we hope to retain after this war is over.
That we would retain a goodly portion of the United Kingdom market was one of the promises made by this government; but when the minister embarked upon his program of subsidy controls and other juggling tricks, many farmers, particularly western farmers, went out of hog production. By 1947 the minister explained to the House of Commons that the target amounts which were the incentive of Canadian production had been replaced in the negotiation of British food contracts by an estimate of the amount which Canadian farmers could supply. I well remember that on that occasion he took pains to explain that this did not represent a paring down by the United Kingdom government, but now he says it did. The truth is that as a result of his manipulation of feed grain subsidies Canada in subsequent years failed to fulfil the British bacon contracts, thereby encouraging and indeed forcing the United Kingdom to seek her bacon elsewhere.
With each downward revision of the contract our exports continued to fall below the stipulated quotas. The minister and his colleagues knew at least two years back, as he admitted in the House of Commons on December 10, 1949, that the United Kingdom would drastically reduce her imports from Canada; yet in the face of that fact the minister stubbornly maintained during the last election campaign that our British markets were not being reduced, but that they were quite normal. That is substantiated by Canadian Press reports of the minister's statements. I quote from a report dated June 23, 1949:
Agriculture minister Gardiner said tonight "There is no evidence" to support the contention of C.C.F. leader Coldwell that Canada is losing the British food market. Mr. Gardiner said, "The evidence is quite the opposite."
Then again on November 18, 1949, he is reported to have said:
"In any conversations I have had with Sir Stafford Cripps and food minister Strachey, I have never gathered the impression they were not prepared to take all the products they could afford to pay for from Canada," Mr. Gardiner said.

The Address-Mr. Charlton
I had the privilege of listening to the minister in Brantford on December 5, when he reached the ultimate in double-talk and selfprotection during his address to the board of trade farmers' night in that city. The minister's remarks seem fairly well explained in an editorial appearing in the Ottawa Journal of December 7. It reads as follows:
Our Minister of Agriculture makes a discovery.
In Brantford on Monday night our Minister of Agriculture, Mr. James Gardiner, told the board of trade there was "a very decided official effort" to drive wheat and other Canadian food products from the British market. Said he: "During the last two years a very decided official effort has been made to drive every one of these products (pork, cheese, beef, eggs, etc.) off the British market. And now that the four-year wheat contract is drawing to a close an effort is being made to drive off a considerable part of our wheat as well."
Sounds more, this, like Erie Stanley Gardner, the detective story writer, than James G. Gardiner, Canadian Minister of Agriculture. But as we must assume there is no case of mistaken identity on the part of the reporter, we feel constrained to ask: If this British official conspiracy against our food products has been going on for two years, how come that Mr. Gardiner just tells about it now? And telling it, not in the House of Commons, where it should have been told, and where Mr. Gardiner could be cross-examined, but to an audience in Brantford.
Not that we ourselves are at all startled by what Mr. Gardiner says. Ordinarily we should be inclined to say to him that at Brantford he said too much or too little, and to tell him that he should identify the British officials who allegedly work against us. What we feel, however, is that what Mr. Gardiner seemingly "revealed" in Brantford was not a revelation at all, but simply that he is now admitting something the British have been saying to us, and quite frankly, for more than a year-things which Mr. Gardiner, like the rest of us, knew all about, but which, because of promises he had made often to many, he stubbornly refused to admit. In other words, all that really has happened is that events have caught up with Mr. Gardiner, making a rubbish-heap of what he and some of his distinguished colleagues tried to tell us, for their own political good, before, during, and since the election.
One part of this very important speech has been missed in this editorial, and that was Mr. Gardiner's statement-very conveniently made, it would seem, in a city such as Brantford, which is one of the greatest implement manufacturing centres in Canada-that being a free trader himself, he would have to advise all farmers to buy where they could sell, in Canada. The only conclusion that could be arrived at from this statement is that the minister is now suggesting a policy of national self-sufficiency. This statement, from a minister of a government pledged to freer expansion of trade, would surely make strange reading to his western supporters.
A later confession of failure was made at the closing session of the tenth annual dominion-provincial agricultural conference held in Ottawa on December 14. I have here an article from the Globe and Mail, a Canadian Press dispatch dated December 15, 1949.

The headline is, "Little bacon, no eggs: U.K. food pact collapses, still chance for cheese." The subheading reads as follows: "Gardiner says outlook dismal for agriculture: Hears price support plea."
The article reads:
Agriculture minister Gardiner today painted a dismal picture of 1950 Anglo-Canadian food contracts.
Of the 1949 contracts for bacon, cheese, eggs, salmon and apples, no contracts appear in sight except for cheese, and even that still is uncertain. Wheat is covered by a two-year agreement which expires next year.
The minister was finding it increasingly difficult to pull these United Kingdom contracts out of the hat just before Christmas. Yet, we have the statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) at Moncton on May 19, 1949, as reported in the Toronto Daily Star. The statement reads as follows:
The outlook today is far brighter than at the end of the war-wherever there are markets to be found for Canadian exports a Liberal government will find them.
Then we have the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture trying his best, under difficult circumstances, to fly a trial balloon at the rural life conference held at the university of Western Ontario on December 28. I quote from a press dispatch appearing in the Globe and Mail on December 29, 1949, which reads as follows:
Farmers would be better without government aid is advice of McCubbin.
An early return to selling Canadian farm products by private enterprise rather than by government contracts was urged today by Robert McCubbin, M.P. for Middlesex West and parliamentary assistant to agriculture minister Gardiner.
"The sooner the dominion government gets out of handling the farmer's products the better the farmer will be in Canada," he told 100 farmers and junior farmers attending a three-day rural life conference at the university of Western Ontario.
"Government contracts were all right during the war, and for the first two or three post-war years, but I feel that now farmers should handle their own farm products," he said.
I remember quite well, Mr. Speaker, that two years after the war was over this party tried its best to persuade the government to get out of the field of business, and let the farmers' organizations handle the products for the producer. The parliamentary assistant's speech sounds very much like a good Conservative speech.

To ask 13 million people to balance trade with 50 million is impossible-it never will be possible. We can never buy as much as we can sell to Great Britain."
Just here, Mr. Speaker, I should like to quole a few of the trade figures with Great Britain and the United States. I might say that during the last four years we have had a lesser plus trade balance with the United Kingdom than we have had a minus balance with the United States. It will be realized that practically every one of those figures shows a greater minus for the United States than a plus for Great Britain. If we cannot be expected to balance our trade with Great Britain, which only has 40 or 50 million people, how can we balance our trade with the United States with 150 million people?
The article from which I was quoting continues as follows:
Apart from the disparity in population there was a second big reason why Canadians would never balance trade with Great Britain, he said. to say:
"Unless we can give them as cheap an egg as other people they will buy from other countries. And the same applies to bacon. If we can produce bacon at a price comparable with other countries, then Britain wants our bacon."
He suggested farm organizations could very well start formulating plans to lower food production costs to meet world and especially western European competition on the European markets.
Is it the parliamentary assistant's suggestion, Mr. Speaker, that the farmers should be singled out as the only group to lower production costs? We realize that we are pricing ourselves out of the European markets; but the same could be said of practically every other industry in this country.
I should be glad if the parliamentary assistant could tell us how to reduce our costs without becoming miners of the soil; and that situation, as I am sure all will agree, is a dangerous one. Farmers are not complaining so much about price reductions as they are about the fact that they alone of all producers are expected to take less income at the present time. As the result of new contract prices and their effect on all domestic prices, farmers face an income drop of between $200 million and $250 million this year from their average of the past two years.
Some serious consideration was given to this rapidly-descending deflated trial balloon put up by the parliamentary assistant. The minister discovered that it was not going to be so easy to throw his worn-out market basket back to the producers when surpluses began to appear and prices began to degenerate. It is the age-old squeeze to which the farmers are expected to submit, but national economics in these modern times are more delicately balanced than they were when the unorganized producers of foodstuffs were merely hewers of wood and drawers of water. Agriculture is an industry now, not only a way of life; and it provides a tremendous market for the goods of our mills and factories. Agriculture, however, provides that market only when it has buying power. By increasing the cost of operation and lessening the income, rural people will be forced to buy less and their plight will soon be reflected in bank clearings, sales and monthly employment figures.
This fact became increasingly evident to farmers, industry and government as unemployment increased rather sharply to levels

Finally, contracts were signed with the United Kingdom for bacon and cheese at greatly reduced prices. In the case of bacon the contract was for 60 million pounds of Wiltshire sides at 29 cents a pound, with a government subsidy of $3.50 a hundredweight; and the contract was for 75 million to 85 million pounds of cheese at 25 cents a pound, f.o.b. Montreal, with a government subsidy of 3 cents a pound.
Our Canadian Cheddar cheese is the best in the world. It constitutes one of the best markets for our surplus milk production. The United Kingdom could and would take more of our cheese; but as I have stated previously in this house, we must modernize our packaging and marketing methods if we hope to hold this market. It is my belief that we should establish a processing and packaging plant in the United Kingdom. When 90-pound Cheddars arrive there, they could be regraded, cut, and packaged as the demand required, and the trimmings could be processed into soft cheese. Certainly we cannot expect to sell our cheese by the same methods we used fifty years ago, against competition from packaged cheese of New Zealand and Australia. It is a question of going out and doing a selling job. It can be done.
The minister states that there is a little surplus of cheese. The total as of March 1, 1950, was 38,613,000 pounds as against 27,873,000 pounds at the same date in 1949, showing an increase of nearly 11 million pounds. What about the 17 million pounds held over by the government from last year? Is it still good or will it have to be sold to processors?
It was not, however, until January 26 that any announcement was made by this government regarding the floor price on eggs. For over a month and a half this government allowed poultry producers to flounder hopelessly. As a consequence whole flocks were liquidated at bargain prices. Ungraded eggs were sold for as little as 16 cents a dozen. The damage has been done, and unless hatchery sales increase considerably in the next two months, consumers will pay dearly for their eggs this fall because of another government blunder. The floor price of 38 cents to dealers, plus at least 4 cents for storage, is no guarantee to the producers. It is only the more efficient who can survive at that figure. Hence the low hatchery orders. In January, for instance, hatchery orders were only 25 per cent of orders in January, 1949. There is little increase in the orders for February. In order to avoid wide fluctuations


in production, the floor price should have been set as nearly as possible to the average cost of production. In this way only the inefficient producer is forced to liquidate his flock, and violent price changes are avoided. This is one contract that was definitely lost, whether the minister admits it or not.
On January 26, while speaking at the convention of the dairy farmers of Canada which I had the privilege of attending, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) tried to justify a 10 million to 20 million pound surplus of butter this spring when the new production season begins. Again last Wednesday he tried to dispel any fears of a little butter surplus and twitted the opposition that it was no more than we had asked for a couple of years ago. I believe the minister realizes all too well that the situation with regard to butter has changed somewhat in the past year. The minister or his government did not have the courage to deal with the margarine issue but passed the buck to the supreme court and from there to the provinces. Now that margarine is on the market, the danger is not a scarcity of butter as it was previously, but a surplus as exists today.
Appearing in the Ottawa Journal of March 3 of this year is an article headed "Six cent slash coming", which reads in part as follows:
Dairy farmers are expected to submit to the government that they should have greater protection against the inroads of margarine. They set forth that in no other dominion is so little assistance given dairymen in saving their industry from the inroads of vegetable oil products.
They submit that their income in 1949, even with the price support program, showed a decline of 12 per cent in the six months ending in September, and if this was spread over a year the loss to Canadian dairy farmers1 would total $46 million. With a reduced butter price the loss would be even greater.
Then a little further on:
The increasing competition offered by cheaper margarine was indicated by January figures showing its consumption in that month totalled 8,152,000 pounds compared with 19,400,000 pounds of creamery butter disappearance.
On February 1, total stocks were reported at 46,500,000 pounds including the 30,000,000 bought by the government under the price support program. This was 12,000,000 pounds more than the previous record for this date and 27,500,000 more than for the same date last year.
Then again, there was a Canadian Press report in the London Free Press of March 10, headed "Production of margarine exceeds creamery butter", which reads in part as follows:
For the first month in history, the production of margarine has exceeded the output of creamery butter.
It happened in February, when butter production in Canada is always at its lowest point for seasonal

reasons. During that month, production of margarine totalled 8,646,000 pounds compared with creamery butter output of 8,494,000 pounds.
On Thursday, March 9, the minister gave a report to the house on the butter situation. I quote from Hansard at page 585:
For the benefit of hon. members I wish to state that the last ten-year average storage of butter, as of March 1, was, in round figures, 19 million pounds. The highest storages as of that date were 23 million pounds1 in 1940 and 24 million in 1947. The storage as of March 1, 1950, is 36 million. Of this amount the government had 25 million pounds.
According to the figures I received from the department the total is a little larger than that, but the difference is not too great, only 578,000 pounds. As a matter of fact that would be considered nothing by this government.
Incidentally I might mention a few other little surpluses which the minister seems to have pushed aside as unimportant. As of January 1, 1950, there were 10 million pounds of honey on hand-a million more than at the same date last year. As far as white beans are concerned, I am sure the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture has heard about the estimated figure of 200,000 bushels above our domestic requirements. The minister might also use the word "little" to describe our potato surplus. Total holdings are only 432,020 tons as of March 1 of this year, the largest amount ever known in this country at this time of year. Translated into bushels it is 17,280,800. It is also interesting to note that to date this year we have exported a total of 3,298,112 bushels of table stock, while the total for last year was only 3,444,965.
The total hold-over at this time this year is 82,625 tons more than last year. These figures are taken from the dominion Department of Agriculture, fruit, vegetable and honey crop market report, No. 49. The figures for this year are 432,020 tons, while the figures for last year were 349,395 tons. That is the total for all Canada. This difference of 82,625 tons amounts to 3,305,000 bushels.
With regard to apples, there is also a little surplus in the country. Let us start with the maritimes. These are cold storage and common storage figures. In 1949 there were 9,111 bushels in cold storage. This year there are 210,165 bushels in cold storage. No doubt if there is a by-election down there shortly they will all be disposed of before that time. I shall not mention all these figures. In Quebec this year there are fewer apples in storage than there were last year. In eastern Ontario there are a great many more than there were last year. In western Ontario there were 229,951 bushels in storage
The Address-Mr. Charlton last year; this year there are 258,783 bushels in cold storage. I remind the house that these are cold storage figures, and do not include common storage. There are many more in common storage as well. The total for all Canada as of March 1, 1950, was 2,332,663 bushels, as against 1,181,308 bushels at the same date last year. The difference is over a million bushels.
The Minister of Agriculture has bungled the agricultural policy of this country. He has laboured to create a condition in which it is most difficult for us to do business with our best customer, and an atmosphere of uneasy mistrust exists between Canada and the United Kingdom. He condemns Canadian farmers to their fate with only a vestige of former markets abroad left to them and no substitutes in sight.
This government has depended too much on ECA funds from the United States supplying the dollars for our United Kingdom markets-a fund which is diminishing rapidly for our use in view of large surpluses in the United States.
The farmers of Canada have paid the premium-a very dear one of over one billion dollars-on a policy of price stability handed to them by this government and accepted. Paid for in advance they now expect that policy to be honoured, not thrown back at them without even a return of premiums paid.
Not all Liberal campaign advertising followed through with what their leaders were saying. I have here an advertisement which appeared in the Prairie Examiner under date of June 13, 1949, in which it seems they were very frank in what they intended to do. Referring to their past policies they said this:
How successfully it tackled that job is charted above. Never have Canada's farm families been so prosperous, so secure. Never have they enjoyed so large a share of the nation's income.
But in referring to the future they say:
Floors under farm prices to assure farmers a minimum guaranteed return; the Prairie Farm Assistance Act to protect grain growers against the hazards of crop failure; long-range programs of conservation.
And so on. Then they say:
These and many other constructive steps reflect the Liberal policy "not only to provide farmers with a minimum of stability and security but also to help them to achieve an ever-increasing prosperity."

No doubt farmers from the west will be surprised to read in Hansard the speeches delivered by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. [Mr Charlton.]
Wright) and the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) in which they protest against the twenty-cent interim payment on grain which was made last spring. Both hon. members suggested it should not have been made, and one said it should have been only ten cents or less. This is a strange attitude for hon. members representing agricultural constituencies. I know that in the southern part of my constituency, where we had three years of crop failure, this twenty-cent payment was an absolute necessity. They pointed out that the government had to borrow money. Naturally it had to; any farmer would be well aware of that situation, because he cannot have grain in his granary and money in the bank at the same time. Until the wheat is disposed of the money would not be available to make payments.
It was also pointed out that the interest charge in connection with this borrowing would be charged against' the farmer. That may be so; but they would have had to go to the bank to borrow it, in any case, and perhaps would not have had as easy a time as the government did. The farmers may have had to borrow the whole amount whereas the government had to borrow only a small portion because it was selling grain from time to time. If the constituents of those hon. members are like mine, then they will have some difficulty in explaining the attitude they have taken in the house.
It was also suggested by the hon. member for Assiniboia that if the farmers had known in June of last year what they know now they would not have voted as they did. I went through my riding during the Christmas season, when they knew considerably more than they did at the time of the election, and I believe that' there were more Liberals at Christmas than there were on June 27. Perhaps that is not because of any action I have taken, or that has been taken by any member of the government; possibly it is more due to the action of the C.C.F. government' in Saskatchewan.
I do not wish to be-unduly hard on hon. members across the floor, because I do not think they subscribe to much of the action taken by the Saskatchewan government. Certainly their attitude in the House of Commons is usually just the opposite to that of the Saskatchewan legislature, as indicated by the action it takes.
The further criticism is made that the twenty-cent payment was made available so as to influence the farmers at the time of the election in June. We realize of course that the system followed by the C.C.F. to exert

influence at election time is somewhat different; but let us not forget that they have ways of influencing the voters.
Mention has been made of the election in The Battlefords, and I do not intend to discuss it in detail. Perhaps I might point out however that the first action taken by the C.C.F. candidate in that campaign was to go on the radio and make the statement that if he won the seat he would spend $200,000 in it. Of course that was done to influence the voters. Then, if we want to go back as far as 1944, we know that many things were said by members of the C.C.F. party to influence the voters.
I well remember that the leader of the C.C.F. spoke in our half at Medstead, where I live. I went to hear him and I must say he made an excellent speech. Referring to the education tax that had been imposed in years of depression by the Patterson government, a tax which had been imposed for educational purposes in those difficult times, he described it as being very bad and said that it was inequitable. Indeed he went on to say that the tax was most iniquitous, and that they were going to take it off.
If it was iniquitous at that time surely it must be more so now. We have just read of the announcement of the Saskatchewan budget, and we find that in that budget the education tax has been increased from two per cent to three per cent. If it was iniquitous in 1944, then the iniquity is now fifty per cent greater.
I do not know whether hon. members have looked over the new Saskatchewan budget, but if they did they would see at once that it runs contrary to the attitude taken by C.C.F. members in this house. They tell us here that we are facing hard times, that we are likely to have a depression, and so on. They always take the stand that things are going to be tough. If that is so, one would expect them to have those thoughts in the back of their minds in Saskatchewan.
Delivering his budget in Saskatchewan it would seem that Mr. Fines said something to that effect. A report in the Regina Leader-Post, referring to Mr. Fines' budget, states this:
"In my opinion," said Mr. Fines, "we have now passed the peak and from now on revenues will decline. I do not anticipate any sudden fall during the next six months but rather a steady gradual decline. What will happen after that time will depend on crop conditions and ability to dispose of our agricultural products at reasonable prices."
In the face of that statement one would expect that he would take some heed of the future. Instead of that however the budget is expanded, showing an increase of some $6 million, from $49 million last year to $55
The Address-Mr. Harrison million this year. Then, if one considers grants from the federal government, compulsory insurance on automobiles and hospital taxes, all of which must be classed as taxes, it is clear that the legislature this year is going to spend in that province about $69 million.
The attitude of the C.C.F. party in Manitoba, where the government is about to spend $39 million, is to the effect that this amount is out of all proportion, and that it is far too high. Yet, in Saskatchewan, with a C.C.F. government, they propose to spend $69 million.
Bearing these thoughts in mind, one finds it hard to reconcile the budget with what the provincial minister of finance says in his budget speech. It is hard to reconcile that budget speech with some of the speeches made by members of the C.C.F. in the House of Commons, wherein they point out that we must expect at least a recession. In brief, this means a contribution of about $80 for each man, woman and child in Saskatchewan, or a total of $400 for the average family of five. It is possible that if we do not continue to have favourable crops such as we have had in the last few years, when they have been fairly good, we will be pricing ourselves out of the land picture. If the tax is not paid the land will be taken over, rather than leave it in the possession of the people who now own it. The net debt as shown by the Saskatchewan budget has been increased by about $3 million, and the new education tax of three per cent will provide an additional income to the province of between $3 million and $4 million.
Some hon. members heard the discussion which took place the other evening following the speech of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) in which he pointed out that the means test was imposed in Saskatchewan on the $2.50 supplementary payment basis. I well remember during the campaign of 1944 seeing placards in my constituency displaying the legends "Humanity first" and "People before profits." These were distributed in considerable quantity. One would wonder at a government supporting those slogans imposing a means test of the kind indicated-and then going out and saying that the means test should be removed.
I, too, believe that that should be done; but certainly they are in a position to do it when it is imposed on only $2.50. Some hon. members may not be aware of this fact, that the share of pensions borne by the Saskatchewan legislature is no more now than it was in 1927, when the scheme was first established. At the same time the income of that government has been trebled. Other provinces, such as British Columbia, have been paying $50 or over. That is what they

The Address-Mr. Harrison believe in and that is what they fought for in this house. Naturally you would think that they would do that in Saskatchewan.

I want to refer to some of the things required in that part of the country. The Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act has proved to be most desirable. Considerable dairying is carried on in my constituency, especially in the southern end, but we are precluded from the benefits of this act because we are outside the Pre-Cambrian shield. The water table in this part of my riding has dropped 25 feet in the last 20 or 25 years and this is causing considerable concern to those engaged in the dairying business. They are faced with the possibility of having to reduce their herds at a time when they should not have to do so. When this matter is up for consideration I shall urge that this act apply not only to territories like my own riding but to the maritimes and other parts of the country. We should get rid of the "prairie" in the title of the act and consider it as a rehabilitation scheme for the whole country.
The hon. member for The Battlefords (Mr. Bater) referred to the curtailment of train service and urged the use of our own coal and oil, particularly by the Canadian National Railways. Some action should be taken to see that our own coal is used, possibly exclusively, even though it meant the payment of additional subsidies. If more of

The Address-Mr. Harrison feel like taking a day off they may do so, or they may have a couple of weeks at the lake, and things are as they should be.
It is possible that these thoughts were in the back of the minds of so many Canadians who were pulling for Winston Churchill in the recent British election. Certainly he could have made a clean sweep in this country if Canadians had been allowed to vote. No doubt they felt he would have insisted upon an approach to Britain's problems as realistic as when he came out with the "blood, sweat and tears" that brought us all through the war. Certainly it will be the hope of every Canadian, especially those in the west, that Britain will soon regain her prosperity, and have her eight-hour day and the odd holiday at the beach, as we and our neighbours across the line are able to do. Until she is able to do this, she will buy from us only what she has to have, or we will have to loan or give it to her. If she will approach her problems realistically she will not And Canada wanting in giving her aid, for by so doing we will help ourselves regain one of our best cash customers. I do not want this house to think I am condemning Britain too severely, but I believe she should face her problems in a different light. I should be one of those in sympathy with her, because I was born there and usually you have a soft spot in your heart for your native land. Certainly I have for mine. I do think, however, she might approach her problems in a different manner and obtain better results.
The answer of the leader of the opposition to our trade problems was to suggest a commonwealth conference. In the light of realities a conference makes little contribution to a solution. As I said before, you would be faced immediately with the question of what to use for money. The leader of the C.C.F. party (Mr. Coldwell) suggested that we should take sterling in payment of our goods. That would have some merit if we were in a position to extend more credit, because that is what it would amount to. Sir Stafford Cripps made that quite plain in an interview reported in the Toronto Star of February 11, when he said:
The acceptance by Canada of sterling instead of dollars would not in itself solve the problem. This really wouldn't solve anything. It would only defer payment. It would really be a Canadian credit given without interest.
That is the long and short of it. The leader of the Social Credit party (Mr. Low) went a little further and suggested that the sterling might be reinvested in empire countries. I thought his proposal had considerable merit; but I am afraid the only country in the world in a position to accept that responsibility is the United States. That is about the only


country with enough money to develop her own economy and have anything left over for development elsewhere. We are in the position of a young fellow just starting in business, who needs all his capital for his own affairs. Canada has much to develop here, and in fact needs outside money in order to proceed with the development of her own resources. Having that in mind I agree with the leader of the Social Credit group that the policy he suggested would be a good thing not only for us but also in the promotion of peace. I am afraid acceptance of that theory, however, is precluded by the fact that we require our money here in Canada.
The picture as to the sale of our agricultural products is not too dark, though it will require thought and wise merchandising by this government, and a realistic approach to her problems by Britain herself. She will buy a great deal from us in any case, but we may have to eventually reduce our acreage in wheat and grow more coarse grains, marketing that as beef in the United States. In other words we will have to make some adjustments. We may have to increase the production of hogs for our own use, because right now we are using about 90,000 per week and are not producing much more than that; and we are not going to be able to fill the small contract we now have with Britain.
The economic outlook for 1950 is one of continuing general buoyancy. Surveys of the research branch of the Department of. Trade and Commerce covering all levels of government and some 17,500 business firms show that this year we will spend over $3,500 million in improvements and expansion of plants. This is always a criterion by which to judge the progress of a nation. This is the largest expenditure on expansion in our history, and represents 22 per cent of the estimated national income, which is expected to reach an all-time high of $16,250 million this year, or about eight times our pre-war income. We are the third largest trading nation in the world, though we only have one-half of one per cent of the population of the world. Per capita we trade three times as much as the United States, and twice as much as Britain. To further diversify and stabilize our economy, great oil fields have been discovered. Add to all this a great national leader in the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), and we can look to the future with confidence.
For my constituents in Meadow Lake I have only one wish to assure their prosperity; that is, that they may be up to their knees in mud about June 1. This, together with the leadership I have mentioned and the proven

policies of the right hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), will assure a high level of prosperity for my constituents.
