speechtext:
The question does not arise, and when the member for Kootenay East makes statements such as the one I quoted from his speech he is parroting Harvey Murphy.
My main reason for taking part in this debate, Mr. Speaker, is to draw the attention of the government to the concern of the people of British Columbia, and the city of Vancouver, with the question of unemployment, as well as other important questions which are now confronting us. With 15-8 per cent of the labour force of the province unemployed, the question of unemployment has reached the proportions of a major emergency. Furthermore, the concern of the people of the province and of my city is increased by the unconcern of the authorities here.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) spoke in this debate he concluded his speech

by reading an editorial which appeared in the Montreal Star and which was headed: "1950, a Year of Adjustment." I think it was fitting that the Prime Minister should conclude his speech by reading a conservative editorial from the most conservative newspaper in Canada, for his own speech was as Conservative as anything I have heard in this house for many years.
That 1950 is likely to be a year of adjustment is one of the reasons why so many people are filled with concern. People are worried because they see the pattern of that adjustment emerging before their eyes, and what they are seeing does not inspire them with hope or confidence in the future. They have experienced similar adjustments in the past and know what they mean in human suffering. They see the cost of living increasing, employment decreasing and, worse still, they see the government throwing overboard the program for full employment and extended social security on which they won two elections. If anything further was required to complete their disillusionment and to increase their fear of the future, the Prime Minister's speech on the address provided it.
To hon. members on all sides of the house may I suggest that the times we are facing require of us that we should give the most searching analysis to the operation of our economic system. In my opinion the functioning of our economy has reached a stage which capitalism in the past has never been able to surmount. I shall explain what I mean. The so-called free enterprise system under which we operate fluctuates between periods of booming production and stagnating depression or, in other words, between high employment and mass unemployment. In boom periods, such as we have had since about 1939, everyone is more or less prosperous. When times are bad, millions are in want. We should try to understand what are the causes of our periods of prosperity and also what are the causes of our periods of depression.
Our periods of prosperity are caused either by supplying war needs, as we have done twice in the last thirty-five years, or a high demand for capital goods for use at home or abroad, or both. The amazing paradox of our system is this. When we have supplied our needs or other people's needs for capital goods, hard times begin. This is just the reverse of what the situation should be in any sane system of production. When our need for capital goods is met, we should then be in a position to start increasing our production of consumers' goods. But paradoxically, the reverse of that happens: we start curtailing the production of consumers' good

The truth of what I have said will be clear to anyone who will take the trouble to analyse the periods of prosperity and depression during the last one hundred years. It has been a succession of booms and busts, with the booms getting shorter and the busts getting longer with each economic cycle. Every time we have reached the stage when we should be in a position to make a mass attack on poverty in order to reduce it and to raise the standard of living of that part of the population which is always living below the line of health and decency, business begins to slow down, opportunities for investment begin to decline, unemployment increases and hundreds of thousands lose all they gained when production was booming. That has been the picture ever since I can remember, and it has been the picture for one hundred years before that. I am convinced that in this year of 1950 we are fast approaching a situation such as the one I have outlined, and that it will shortly overtake us unless something is done quickly to prevent it.
What can be done? Profiting by the lessons of the great depression and the knowledge of what we demonstrated we could do during the war, when as a people we had a national objective and a common purpose, the government in 1945 in a white paper outlined what they thought the future government policy had to be if we were to avoid the ups and downs which have always plagued our economy. On Thursday evening the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) dealt with the salient points of the white paper, and I will not repeat what he said. I believe, however, hon. members will agree with me that the proposals contained in the white paper were worth-while aims. The authors of that document were aware of the fact that the social essentials mentioned therein, namely, opportunity, welfare and security, were lacking for hundreds of thousands of Canadians in the decade before 1939. Furthermore, by the achievements in production during the war, they were convinced that that lack was unnecessary. I am satisfied that that was the reason why we had the white paper.
The government itself placed a great deal of importance on that document at the time it was issued. On April 12, 1945, when the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), then minister of reconstruction, tabled the document he had this to say, and I quote from page 808 of Hansard of 1945. It may have no significance whatever, but I may mention that April 12, 1945, was the day before parliament prorogued; it was
The Address-Mr. Maclnnis later dissolved and we had the election of that year. The then minister of reconstruction is reported as follows:
Mr. Speaker, acting in my capacity as minister of reconstruction, I desire to lay on the table of parliament a statement on government policy, having to do with employment and income, with special reference to the initial period of reconstruction.
I commend this document to you as deserving careful study. It is perhaps the most important government document that has been presented to this parliament in recent months.
It is regrettable that the government so soon forgot its importance. Then he went on to show some of the things that were to be done. I am now quoting from page 810 of Hansard:
A co-ordinator of public projects will stimulate the planning of public works and map out the timing and nature of government expenditures on public works projects. The purpose will be to have in hand at all times a shelf of public projects already planned and available when needed to stimulate employment in any given area.
We were told by the Prime Minister the other day that unemployment was spotty; that it' was localized. That is just exactly what the proposals and the program outlined in the white paper were intended for, so that as soon as unemployment showed itself in any locality plans would be ready to provide for it.
I continue with the quotation:
In order to keep the department in close touch with every part of Canada, local regional councils have been appointed, one in each province of Canada, and two in the large industrial provinces of Ontario and Quebec. These committees will have a permanent executive staff. The duty of the committees will be to keep the department informed of employment conditions in their respective areas, to recommend public projects suitable for their area, and to keep citizens within their area informed about the work of the department. These committees will be representative of the various economic groups within the area, and will include representatives of labour.
I have one or two other short sentences and I shall be finished with these proposals, the outline of which was given so dramatically by the minister of reconstruction on the date I mentioned. I continue:
The need for immediate and extensive reconstruction measures has not yet arisen, but the machinery is ready, and action will be prompt whenever we enter into the period of transition following the defeat of Germany. However, the machinery cannot operate without a comprehensive policy to guide it in its working, and set the targets for it. Here also the pattern has been set, the principles have been agreed upon, and the way cleared for action.
The way was cleared but no action was taken. In the last paragraph we have this:
To attempt to summarize the document would be an invitation to hon. members to avoid giving study to the document itself. Therefore, I will not attempt such a summary. Once again let me urge you to read and study this important statement of government policy.

The Address-Mr. Maclnnis

speechtext: Did the government ever study it?

speechtext:
I doubt very much whether the minister ever looked at it after it' was tabled. Perhaps they did, because later some of the proposals in the green book seem to have been taken from the white paper. Certainly, now is the time when they should put these policies into effect, because there are many places where they are needed.
We have been living in troubled times since the end of the war; but nevertheless in nearly all of the countries of the world, and particularly in the democratic countries, there has been a tremendous increase in production. I noted in a publication a few days ago that in the Marshall aid countries of Europe, with the exception of Germany, production had reached 130 per cent of pre-war. In all of the countries of western Europe shortages are disappearing, and on this continent they are disappearing also. Those who now go without the things they need go without them because they have not the money to buy and not because the goods they need are not available.
I have a feeling that the ease with which the transition was made from war production to peace production has lulled this government into a false sense of security. They seem to have forgotten how capitalism works. They seem to have forgotten the depression of the 1930's, and the events which led up to it. That they have forgotten or refuse to see is apparent from their insistence that the present high unemployment is due to the weather. But to show that there are other and more fundamental reasons for the unemployment, I shall quote from the Prime Minister's speech in this debate at page 53 of Hansard. He said:
About eight or nine months ago, as hon. members know, there was an indication of some slackening of economic activity in the United States. Our pulp and paper people felt that it would be a prudent thing to reduce the size of their inventories in which so much of their working capital was tied up at rather high costs of production,
I am informed the result was that this year there were about 35,000 fewer jobs in the woods than in previous years. That does not mean unemployment merely for 35,000 men.
The Prime Minister went on to show that many workers in other industries were thrown out of work because of the so-called prudent action of the managers of the pulp and paper industry.
When the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Poulin) spoke in this debate last week he showed what happened to the men who supplied the wood to the pulp and paper people. I read from the English translation of the hon. member's speech. He said:
I admit these production costs are rather high, but the companies have reduced their inventories.

He was referring to the statement made by the Prime Minister. I continue:
They have not omitted, however, to reduce, in a shameful manner, the price paid to small operators for pulpwood, and the salaries paid to woodcutters for job work. In view of the price the paper companies get for pulp, it really is a shame that they should be allowed to pay these forest labourers the meagre wage they force them to accept with a knife at their throat, if I may say so.
The knife at their throat is the fear of hunger, the fear of unemployment. I am drawing attention to this quotation, Mr. Speaker, from the Prime Minister's speech and also from the speech of the hon. member for Beauce, because first they show the unemployment is not wholly due to the weather; and second, they show on what a slender thread the livelihood of the people rests under the so-called free enterprise system.
In my home city I do not find any of that easy optimism which flows so easily in the speeches of the Prime Minister. Authorities in Vancouver are convinced that unemployment is due to a slowing down of business. They know that unemployment is worse this winter than it was last; and they are afraid it will be worse next winter than it is this, unless planned action is taken to prevent it.
I hold in my hand a copy of a brief sent to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) by the city council of Vancouver. I shall read from it two short paragraphs to show how the city council of that city looks at this question of unemployment. It reads:
This situation cannot be referred to as unique or surprising, considering the fact that just prior to the last war our economy was reeling from the worst depression known to our country. On the contrary, the last great depression served to make our people and their government more aware of the hardships of an unplanned legislative approach to the emergency which arises when an economic recession sets in. This public consciousness grew and in fact became international when it culminated in the recommendations put forward for the benefit of the peoples of the world and incorporated in the United Nations charter.
The heartening factor to the working classes of Canada, even before the recent overwhelming victory of the government in the last election, was the publicly expressed desire and plans to overcome the unemployment situation which is critical at the present time. These sentiments so expressed with apparent sincerity no doubt accounted for the said overwhelming victory at the polls.
The sentiments to which they refer are the proposals outlined in the white paper and in the speeches by members of the government made afterwards.
I, too, have a letter which I should like to read into the record. This letter is written by a man who for many years has had the job of trying to help those who fail in the day-to-day struggle of earning a livelihood. I believe this letter is far more realistic in its evaluation of present conditions than the editorial read into the record by the Prime

Minister when he spoke. This man sees life from its seamy side. He comes in contact with people who are the first to feel the effects of hard times. I shall not read the whole of the letter, but I am sure the condition this man outlines as being the case in Vancouver is the case in every large centre in Canada. He says:
We are writing, however, to ask you to strive for immediate action to provide financial assistance for families of unemployed persons who at the moment are not eligible for unemployment insurance . . . No assistance to cover food, shelter and fuel for this group is available at the present time in Vancouver. The high cost of living and housing problems, in our experience, make it impossible for families of average income to maintain proper standards of health and decency, and at the same time to put anything by for a rainy day. With jobs not available, savings gone and the breadwinner categorically rejected as ineligible for any assistance, unemployed citizens of Vancouver are now forced to rely upon their grocer, landlord and neighbours, or go the rounds for hand-outs.
It seems unspeakable that in 1950, in the third largest city of Canada, veterans' and non-veterans' families are suffering while our three governments disclaim responsibility for action. As you probably know, in 1945 the federal government framed a comprehensive scheme for unemployment assistance, the provincial statutes of this province include permissive legislation covering assistance, and the city of Vancouver charter sets forth the responsibility for providing for its poor and destitute. Yet, year after year, as unemployment mounts, more families are left without the basic necessities of life.
Then he shows the consequences of this neglect. Referring to the family welfare bureau of greater Vancouver he states:
This organization for twenty-two years has stood for strengthening family life, and we regard the present impasse as both unnecessary and alarming. We know how insidiously under-nourishment, fear and desperation are undermining the physical and mental health of parents and children. In turn these will result in greatly increased public costs in combating physical and mental illness and delinquency in all its varied forms.
I am sure if the editor of the Montreal Star had had the job of looking after these people he would not be so optimistic as he appeared in that editorial to be.
I should like to have made some comment on the amazing speech delivered by the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Mutch) in the debate, but time does not permit. May I point out however that the hon. member seems to have more than his share of fear. He is afraid of statism, whatever that is. He has a congenital distrust of planners-and my understanding of "congenital" is that it is something with which he was born. He has a holy horror of the welfare state, and looks with a jaundiced eye upon subsidies in any form. I do not know whether this completes his list of phobias, but I believe hon. members will agree with me that a man who is prey to
The Address-Mr. Maclnnis so many fears is in no condition to make a full and objective study of the problems confronting our world today.

In conclusion I would urge the government and the members of this house to get back to the thinking that produced the white paper-yes, and later the thinking that produced the green book proposals. Not only should we get back to the thinking but to the spirit of the times when we were all working for a common, national objective. Until we go forward to that stage, where we are thinking in terms of co-operation, and not everyone for himself, we shall not meet effectively those problems which today confront us on every hand.
Any policy based on the assumption that so-called free enterprise will permanently, or even over a relatively long period of time, provide full employment, is bound to lead to disaster. Capitalism will provide employment only so long as substantial profits can be made. This condition applies only in periods of scarcity. It always breaks down in times of plenty. If we are capable of profiting by the experience of the past we must without delay formulate and put into operation policies which will demonstrate to our people that the harder they work, the more they produce, the more secure their lives will be. Indeed the opposite of that is the feeling that they have today where plenty breeds poverty 'and misery.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I should like to take this opportunity to congratulate the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. The way the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Larson) and the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Dumas) acquitted themselves has brought honour not only to themselves but also to the constituencies they represent. I should like also to

The Address-Mr. Decore pay tribute to the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Harris) on his elevation to the very important position of Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. As a new member of this house I am sure I am expressing the sentiments of most new members here when I sayi the minister has been very kind in giving us guidance in our new surroundings and encouragement in our new responsibilities. Being an Albertan-and incidentally, regardless of the Social Credit government, my province is still known as sunny Alberta-I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Prudham) on his appointment as parliamentary assistant. Those of us who know him well are familiar with his ability and honesty, and we know he will carry out his duties effectively and conscientiously. We hope that in the not too distant future he will be given even greater responsibilities which will enable him to take a more active part in the affairs of this country.
I am not going to talk too much about my constituency, except to say what I suppose most hon. members already know, that the constituency I have the honour to represent includes the biggest oil sector in Canada, the famous Redwater oil field. In my constituency we have very progressive farmers, who for the last number of years have gained world recognition of their efforts. Last year the farmers of Vegreville constituency managed to capture three major awards at the Toronto royal fair and the Chicago world show.
In recent days, and indeed over the last few years, we have heard repeated statements by some members on the opposition side of this house as well as other people throughout the land to the effect that a major depression is just around the corner and that this country is heading into economic ruin. While we must be on our guard, such utterances by these calamity howlers certainly are not in the best interests of this country. In this connection I should like to direct attention to an editorial which appeared recently in the Montreal Gazette; and I chose the Gazette for a specific reason, because we all know this particular newspaper supports certain political views in this country:
Ford Head Haps Calamity Howlers
A useful and timely public declaration was made in Toronto yesterday by Mr. Rhys M. Sale, the recently appointed new president of the Ford Motor Company of Canada. He spoke out firmly against the dangers and lack of real basis in the tendency in some quarters to fear and foretell a business depression in the next two or three years. He confessed with good reason to being worried to see "professional gloom-spreaders doing their best to talk us into a depression."
Mr. Sale was rightly concerned that, even without any valid foundation or signs of economic collapse, the talk of such calamity howlers could engender public apprehension which, in itself, could bring

on business stagnation and instability. Evidence presented by public opinion polls and otherwise indicated an initial undercurrent of unjustified fear akin to the panic which largely contributed to the depression of the 1930's.
The motor company head saw "not the slightest" ground for the kind of fear being stirred by "some opportunists" and by scare reports on current economic problems which, while real, had hardly brought the country to the brink of disaster. He pointed to Canada's continuing increase in population, in capital investment and creation of new wealth, and the high level of personal earnings, as some of the factors warranting a firm confidence in the future, whatever moderate or temporary adjustments there might be from time to time in the business tempo.
We all realize that we are now in a transitional period, passing from a wartime to a peacetime economy. That is bound to be reflected in conditions throughout Canada. During the war it was quite an easy matter for us to dispose of our surplus products, especially agricultural products, because the whole world wanted our wheat, our bacon, our beef, and whatever we had to sell. But gradually the economies of the European countries are being adjusted, and of course we are experiencing certain difficulties. However, I repeat that Canada has no room for calamity howlers and gloom-spreaders. It seems to me some of these people almost wish there would be a major economic depression so that eventually they would be in a position to say "I told you so." My submission is that if they continue to spread fear and distrust their efforts might very well bear fruit and bring about a depression.
At this time I should like to draw the attention of hon. members to the matter of the trans-Canada highway. I appreciate that legislation in this regard was put through last session, and I do not want to create the impression that I am dealing with a dead issue or whipping a dead horse. However, I do not believe the question of the trans-Canada highway has been settled, especially in the prairie provinces. I am referring to the route, Of course. As a representative from northern Alberta you would naturally expect me to favour the Yellowhead route; and for that I offer no apologies. However, I prefer to look at the matter not merely as one coming from the town of Vegreville or as an Albertan or even as a westerner, but rather from the Canadian point of view. I am not casting any reflection upon any government, but I do not believe for a moment that any of the provincial governments in western Canada are competent to decide the route on a national basis. Naturally they will be guided by provincial rather than national considerations.
The question of the trans-Canada highway route is of great importance to the Dominion of Canada from the point of view of defence. We realize that we are going to spend large

sums of money for defence purposes this year. Again, the question of where this trans-Canada highway is to go plays an important part in our defence. I have been told that the three most westerly provinces seem to favour the Calgary-Kicking Horse route. If I were satisfied that the decision to have the highway go through Calgary and Banff had been made by competent persons with full knowledge of the relevant facts as to alternative routes, then I would be prepared to abide by such a decision. But I am not satisfied.
At the moment, I believe the Calgary-Kicking Horse route is only second best, and a poor second, when compared with the Yel-lowhead route. A reference was made today by the member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) to a rat, and the important role that that rat landing in Edmonton would play in coming from the east and blazing a trail for the trans-Canada highway. An interesting question arises as to why this rat, instead of going through Medicine Hat and that part of the country, stopping over at Calgary, by way of the Kicking Horse pass, in which there are hundreds of miles of desert, arid land, sand, cactus and no water, chose to go to Edmonton. I think the answer is quite simple. Even a rat knows better.
On a prior occasion the member for Calgary West referred to Edmonton, and said he never knew about Edmonton until he heard of a little place called Leduc. It was Leduc that put Edmonton on the map. He went on to say that, so far as Edmonton was concerned, for miles around Edmonton there was nothing but swamp. It so happens that takes in part of my constituency, and I must confess that I have been getting complaints from some of my constituents about it. I should like to say that those of us who come from that part of Alberta have a high regard for the member for Calgary West. He is held in high esteem and, of course, we realize his ability in this chamber. But as you know, at times most of us have to go through certain misfortunes. We are bound to do certain things we do not like to do. It appears to be the unfortunate lot of the hon. member for Calgary West to have to represent a portion of that cow town called Calgary.

They either go out in the country, or they go to what is now rapidly becoming a suburb of Edmonton, Calgary.

The advantages of the evergreen highway have been listed by the Yellowhead route association. The most important of them are as follows:
1.	The evergreen highway is particularly important at this time as a potential military highway. It connects central Canada with the Alaska highway most directly, and also with Vancouver and Prince Rupert. I think, Mr. Speaker, that is very important. It is certainly something that should be taken into consideration. Again I suggest the provinces are not competent enough to decide this question of defence from a national point of view.
The article continues:
2.	The evergreen highway would prove to be the finest motor tourist highway in the west. It would link four great national parks, and five splendid provincial parks, from east to west. Its whole length would run through beautiful country, wooded, parklike, and gently rolling; not through hundreds of miles of flat prairie with scarcely a tree in sight. It would attract tourists far into the country, keeping them in Canada for longer "spending" periods.
3.	The evergreen highway would cost less to maintain, particularly through the Rockies, for the Yellowhead pass is lower. Its altitude is 3,717 feet compared with the 5,337 of the Kicking Horse pass and the 4,450 of the Crowsnest.

Snowfall on the Yellowhead route also is less. Mud, rock and know slides in the Kicking Horse pass are a constant threat, while in the Yellowhead they are not, for the pass there is much wider.

Now, if I may go back to that rat again, which found its way into Edmonton, they

Although the proposal is that the province pay half of the cost, and the federal government the other half, the fact remains that 100 per cent of the cost of construction and maintenance will have to come out of the pockets of the Canadian taxpayers. The Canadian taxpayer is concerned, and should be concerned, to see that the money spent on this national project is spent to the best possible advantage of this great country of ours. Again I stress the matter of defence. It has been emphasized before, and I am stressing it again, that there should be some fact-finding board or, in the alternative, a royal commission appointed by the federal government to investigate all phases of the construction of the trans-Canada highway. As an alternative, an independent board could be appointed by the federal and provincial authorities to investigate the question of a route for this highway from Winnipeg to Vancouver. The enormous cost of the work, plus the effect it will have on our whole Canadian economy, makes it necessary that the matter be determined not only impartially, but also on a national rather than a provincial level.
I believe the question of the route of the trans-Canada highway, from the point of view of national defence, national development, and national economy, is of vital concern, not only to the people of Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia, but to all Canadians, regardless of whether they are in Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia or any other part of Canada.

speechtext:
I rise, Mr. Speaker, with a great deal of difficulty to take part in this debate. I was in a difficult curling match yesterday, and I find myself stiffened up in quite a few muscles.
This afternoon the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) put on Hansard the record of production in the British isles since 1938 and said that the production this year was 138 per cent' of production in 1938. We all agree that Britain needs that added production. He left the impression, however, that it was as a direct result of the Labour government regime that this increased production came about'. I have here a statement

written by Mr. Alfred Edwards, a member of parliament in Great Britain; he was a Labour member during the last regime. This is what he has to say:
. . . let us look at coal under nationalization and steel under private enterprise. Heaven knows coal under private ownership was no model. England's plight was desperate and she needed full production. So the Labour party took over the mines for the people and voted the equivalent of $100 million for mechanization to increase the per capita production of the worker. Yet from June to October, 1948, in spite of the increased mechanization and in spite of the fact that it is now the people's coal-not that of the greedy capitalists- the mines produced 158,000 tons per week less than in 1938.
He goes on to say that most of the privately run industries have shown a large increase in production since 1945 but coal actually shows a loss. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, it has become a laughing stock in Great Britain. One of the cartoonists has pictured a miner talking to the minister and saying: You told us that under socialism we would get more money for less work. Well, we have given you less work. How about giving us more money? He also says:
The next target for socialism is steel. This is by all tests the most efficient industry in England- perhaps in the world. It produced 11 million tons in 1938, more than 15 million tons in 1948 with but little increase in its mechanization. It has not had a strike in thirty years. Its wages rise and fall according to an agreed arrangement in relation to prices.
This is in striking contrast to the impression left by the hon. member for Vancouver East this afternoon. It looks a great deal as though Britain has made great advances not because of the Labour government but in spite of it.
From there I should like to go to another nationally run concern, and this time one here in Canada. Since the reduction in railway service was put into force-and I am exceedingly glad to see that the regular runs are in operation again-I have received numerous letters and resolutions. I shall not take the time to put any of them on the record word for word, but they ask for an investigation into all of the details; that is, into whether or not there was a coal shortage, and if there was, why; into the effect of the curtailment on the mail, l.c.l. service and express, the loss of business to busses and to the C.P.R.; and into the employment situation as it was affected at that time.
The minister dealt with the matter in part, as reported at page 23 of Hansard, when he said that the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways, at its meeting in October, 1948, approved an objective of 2,365,000 tons of coal for stockpile as at December 31, 1949. As the result of Mr. Vaughan's instructions to cut it down to three

months' supply, the stockpile as of December 31, 1949, was 1,043,000 tons. If the minister had studied the matter he would have found that the suggested stockpile came to something like 532,000 tons of coal per month; that is, for four and a half months' supply. If the stockpile had been up to Mr. Vaughan's suggestion for three months we would have had in the stockpile one-third again as much coal as we had at the end of December. That extra third would have much more than taken care of the 25 per cent reduction in passenger service that was implemented by the C.N.R.
The minister gave us the relative mileages of the C.P.R. and the C.N.R. in eastern Canada, central Canada and western Canada, and he pointed out that the largest mileages of the C.N.R. were in central Canada where no coal supplies were available. What he neglected to say was that the Canadian National Railways serve the Brazeau collieries in Alberta as well as the collieries at Mountain Park, Cadomin, Nacmine, Luscar, and various other coal mining centres. We could go on and name others. We have the Drum-heller and Camrose mines, all served by the Canadian National Railways. I should say, of course, that the coal from some of these mines is not suitable as steam coal but in a good many cases it is. During January I had the pleasure of spending some time in Mirror, which is the divisional point which serves Brazeau. While I was down at the station there I looked over the bulletin for trains; and believe it or not, there were no coal cars available to run into the Brazeau mine. Trains were running out of Brazeau under tonnage; and the Brazeau mines laid off 27 men in the month of January. The mines were there; the coal was there; the will to produce was there, and in a national emergency I would think that not only would the trains be running with full tonnage, but there would be extra trains put on. Where were the coal cars? Alberta has coal reserves of 46 billion tons. If they had wanted the coal we could have given it to them; and that also applies to the great mines in the maritimes. The great Cape Breton mines are served by the Canadian National Railways.
I would suggest that a complete investigation be made into the trans-Canada freight service to determine whether or not the full possible tonnage was being carried between the Alberta coal mines and central Canada, and between the maritime mines and central Canada, and to see whether or not full advantage was being taken of the possibilities and of the reserves of these two parts of the country. The damage that has been done by cutting down this service cannot be estimated.
The Address-Mr. Thomas
During the depression the Canadian National Railways cut off a part of the service between Edmonton and Calgary on Nos. 13 and 14 through Mirror, and Nos. 25 and 26 through Drumheller. That was only temporary, but in that instance it was a financial necessity; at least these lines were never restored to full service. They never needed full service again because as soon as the Canadian National Railways took off that service the Canadian Pacific service between Edmonton and Calgary had to put on extra trains. The Greyhound busses increased, and every little town has a fleet of trucks. The damage can never be repaired.
I have received numerous resolutions from various branches of the Canadian Legion in my constituency, and I should like to put one of them on the record at this time. This is from branch No. 229 Millet, Alberta, and reads as follows:
Millet branch of the Canadian Legion, B.E.S.L. No. 229 heartily concur in the following:
First, the paramount need for a basic increase in war veterans' allowance;
Second, the crying necessity to bring widows and wives completely under the War Veterans Allowance Act to accord them the same benefits as the male recipients;
Third, the importance of setting up a special parliamentary committee on veterans affairs.
I think the basic allowance is now $40.41 for a single man, and $70.83 for a married man. These veterans are being paid for the burning out they received during the first war. They are being paid for services rendered, and it seems a pity that they should be penalized to the extent that they are now getting less than the old age pension. I would strongly urge the minister to consider increasing the basic allowance for a single man to $50 and to $85 for a married man. This would be in accordance with the recommendations of service organizations throughout Canada.
Another point has to do with the widows of the recipients of those allowances. At the present time so long as they have a husband partially to support them they are in receipt of a supplementary allowance, but as soon as their husbands die they are penalized to such an extent that they get nothing.
I would strongly urge that the means test be abolished with reference to those in receipt of the war veteran's allowance, or at least raised to the minimum of the income tax exemption.
There is another group of veterans who deserve a great deal more consideration than they have been getting. We hope that the measure now on the order paper to give the imperial veterans the war veteran's allowance will be passed. I have in mind a man who came over here in 1919 and who has worked

The Address-Mr. Thomas hard to raise his family. He has been an A-l citizen ever since, and at the present time he is getting a basic allowance of $8.41.
I should like to add my plea to the many that have been expressed to give the veterans clear title under the Soldier Settlement Act. Last summer I was approached by one old soldier who had been unable to keep up his interest payments and was unable to pay anything down on the capital because of a bit of tough luck. He owed them $2,000, so he had to get off his land. As soon as he got off, that land was sold to another settler for $800, including improvements.
What is more, I say all this could be done without any further taxation. It could be done out of the wealth of the country. I see some hon. members shaking their heads. Possibly they will remember that the Minister of Finance said that money came as a result of production. I cannot entirely agree with the minister on that. At the present time money is the result of the producer's ability to pay back a loan with interest after he has paid for his own livelihood out of his production. During 1948 production in Canada was estimated at $1,250 per capita. It was also estimated at the same time that the available purchasing power in Canada was $1,000 per capita, thus leaving a discrepancy of $250 per capita short of having enough money to purchase what we produce.
All the federal government has to do to pay for all these things, and to put forth an immense social service campaign, is to issue debt-free money and place it in circulation so as to maintain. a proper balance between our production and our purchasing power.
May I leave one thought in the minds of the government in connection with the payment of family allowances? At the present time these payments begin at birth and end just when a child is reaching a stage of advanced education and requires money most. I suggest that the payment of these family allowances should be continued until a child has finished its education or quits school.
May I say a few words about the subamendment moved by the leader of the C.C.F. party. The proposed amendment to subparagraph (2) of the Progressive Conservative amendment is expressed in broad general terms. This part might be considered to state the objective toward which we are all working, an economy wherein all our people are ensured social justice.
It appears to envision an economy so organized that every Canadian can be assured of adequate food, clothing, and shelter limited only by Canada's productive capacity. Nothing is said as to the method by which the objective shall be reached. We are left, therefore, to fill in the details of method as we

think they should be applied to ensure that social security for Canadians is realized. We favour the broad objective, and we propose to support this subamendment, reserving the right to say by what means we shall attempt to achieve over-all social security for the Canadian people. We want to make it clear that we do not believe it is possible to attain adequate social security by schemes of nationalization, or socialization. And if it has to depend in the main upon taxation we shall never realize social justice in this country. I am confident that we can produce a great enough volume of goods and services that every Canadian can have plenty to eat and wear and to keep him warm, comfortable, and happy. I am also perfectly sure that, through the application of wise reforms in our distribution system, a just over-all level of social security is possible.
As to the second part of the subamendment, we think it is so vaguely worded that it might mean one thing or it might mean another. We interpret it to mean that the government should have pursued a vigorous policy of curbing communism and fascism in Canada, and while doing so, to respect fully the rights and freedoms of individual Canadians.
In dealing with all such movements the appropriate and effective method of attack is to remove undesirable living conditions in Canada. Certainly the government has far too long neglected to apply a remedy to the outrageous cost of living in Canada. Therefore we propose to support this part of the subamendment also. As I said before, we shall support it, but we reserve the right to choose our own methods as to the way in which it should be carried out.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I had determined to tell the house of the beauties of the constituency of Burnaby-Richmond, and the abilities of its people.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What about the weather?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The weather is good, too. However, I propose to tell the house tonight something about what our people are thinking-in fact what people are thinking not only in the House of Commons but everywhere in Canada. We hear from time to time, and we see in the newspapers, statements regarding the President of the United States and his authority to manufacture the hydrogen bomb. We wonder why in this age of modern learning it is necessary at this stage of our development to start on a crusade of destruction, when there should be no need for it.
It seems that our people are thinking, and that everyone in this building tonight is thinking, of what can be done to stop the carnage before it gets started. We believe that the

cemeteries of Europe are full enough of Canadian dead. We feel something should be done-indeed we know something should be done to stop any further battles before they begin.
The situation in the world today seems to be one of fear, and there is some reason for it. We have just witnessed the conquest of China by Russia, and in a moment I shall quote some figures to prove that Russia is now embarked upon a series of conquests, and that we are not prepared to take care of that situation when it develops.
I should like to quote from Newsweek of March 13, referring particularly to an item headed "How we stack up against Russia." As everyone knows, Canada's future is tied up with that of the United States. This article in Newsweek states:
The United States army today consists of ten divisions, including one armoured division and one airborne. Man for man, these divisions have a great deal more firepower than any of the outfits of the last war; they are fairly well trained, and their morale is high. Except for the 82nd airborne and some infantry units in Japan, however, the army is undermanned and underequipped. In contrast, the Red army is believed to have between 150 and 170 divisions, including perhaps 30 armoured divisions, all of them at fighting strength.
The United States air force consists of 48 groups, with roughly 3,300 combat planes and 5,500 transport and support- planes in operation. The Red air force has about 9,000 combat planes ^nd perhaps 8,000 transport and supply planes. More than half of the Russian combat planes are jets; about 300 are TU-4s, a long-distance bomber much like the American B-29.
The United States navy has 7 large carriers, 8 smaller carriers, 1 battleship, 13 cruisers, 140 destroyers, 70 submarines, and 414 other craft in the active fleets. The Red navy has 3 battleships, 14 cruisers, 110 destroyers, about 270 submarines-
And a force of over a thousand vessels in support.
That is the situation in bare outline. The details make it rosy in some respects and blacker in others. As I said, the Canadian future is tide up with the future of the United States. I believe and my people believe that there is no necessity to bring these two great forces into conflict. We believe that if ordinary brains are used-surely we have them in high places-and men from the top level meet around the table, in the end the world will be better off.
It may be said that Russia has refused to keep its obligations in the past. That may be true, but we believe that one more try should be made so that the world may be kept from the destruction that will follow if we go on the way we are. Scientists have told us that if the H-bomb is used at this time it will start a chain reaction that will put civilization into chaos for 500 years; there will be no living on earth. Other scientists tell us that the
The Address-Mr. Goode H-bomb will never be used. There seems to be confusion, not only at the public level, on the part of the man in the street, but in the minds of scientists and government officials.
Before the British elections Mr. Winston Churchill said that if his party was elected he would call a conference at top level immediately to see that Russia and the western democracies were brought together and some type of solution arrived at. Unfortunately- perhaps fortunately for some-that conference will not take place in the near future. My suggestion is that Canada should institute this meeting. We have men of ability who have proved themselves in the United Nations to have what it takes to do this job. Canada should take the lead in bringing Russia and the great powers together to stop this great holocaust.

Mr. Speaker, I did not take part in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne last session, so speaking now in this debate I wish first to congratulate you upon your elevation to the honourable office you now occupy in this house. I want to comment upon the fairness of your decisions during this and the previous session. It is customary for speakers in this debate to congratulate the mover (Mr. Larson) and the seconder (Mr. Dumas), and in offering my congratulations I shall not attempt to add adjectives to those that have been used already. It would be just a repetition of the good things that have been said of these hon. members in connection with the impression they have made with their first speeches. In my humble opinion they did a good job with the text they had to work with.
I should like to take advantage of this opportunity to congratulate the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black) upon his return to the house after an absence on account of illness of three or four weeks. The hon. member is first, last and always working in the interests of the maritime provinces. He is not here at the moment, but I want to say that I am glad to see him back and I hope his health will permit him to remain during the rest of the session.
There are many subjects referred to in the speech from the throne but this debate permits a member to speak on any subject, to travel far and wide without being taken to task for irrelevancy. Any remarks made by an hon. member during this debate cannot be considered to reflect in any way upon the private or public life of His Excellency. His Excellency simply read a document which was placed in his hands by his political advisers.

The Address-Mr. McLure
The speech from the throne is vague and full of pious hopes. I have listened to many of the speeches that have been delivered during this debate and have read others when I did not have the pleasure of being present when they were delivered, and I am fully persuaded that this speech from the throne is exceptionally vague and full of pious and porous hopes. I do not intend to follow the many speeches that have been made, but there are a few remarks to which I may have to refer.
In preparing the speech from the throne the government apparently recognized its unfavourable position. It indicated the weakness of the government to cope with the various situations that exist. It seemed to be an effort to forestall criticism by His Majesty's loyal opposition. The government seems to be quite orthodox because apparently it believes in making a full confession thinking that will be good for its soul. This'speech from the throne is a clumsy exhibition of an effort to befuddle the public. It indicates complete confusion and failure to grapple with the grave situations which are overtaking this country, which are now ripening and bringing about climaxing hardships.
The two main causes of the hardships that exist in this country are unemployment and the lack of markets for our agricultural products. The remedies suggested by the government in the speech from the throne are not good enough to take care of the situation. For instance, widening the scope of the unemployment insurance legislation will not take the place of good jobs. Promises made before and during the last election campaign of undertakings which would provide employment, even if immediately effective, would not give our unemployed what they deserve at the present time. What has the government to offer with respect to unemployment? As I said a moment ago, they said they would widen the scope of the Unemployment Insurance Act.
Let us go a little further and look at something else which is causing great hardship throughout the country. What about the farmers' products? They are packed away in cellars and storage houses across this country, although the government promised to market them. Today the government knows full well that many of these products of the soil are unsalable at the present time, even at prices far below the cost of production.

Well, if you do not know you cannot have been listening to what has been going on here for the last three weeks. The government knows better than I can tell them what those products are, and that they cannot


be sold at anything like the cost of production. During the election campaign the government promised to find markets for our agricultural products, but have they done so? They have not. All they offer the farmer now is sympathy. They say to him, practically in these words, "Live, horse; grass will grow sometime." Addressing the meeting of the Ontario Liberal association in Toronto on April 7, 1949, the then minister of reconstruction and supply (Mr. Winters) is reported as follows in the Globe and Mail of April 8:
Federal government departments have shelved a number of public projects which would act as a bulwark if depression threatened.
He is further reported as having said that these projects would provide employment when needed and would promote the general economic welfare. Of course you realize, Mr. Speaker, that this was election propaganda, which it was hoped would bring results when the voting took place. At the same time the minister referred to different works in different departments. This assurance, so glamorously announced by the minister and consistently nodded to by his cabinet colleagues, brought many a vote at the testing time on June 27.
Now let us look for a moment at this shelf of public works. Perhaps those works were shelved so solidly they have not been able to bring them out.yet. As we look across the country we find a great many people now unemployed. The latest statistics give the total as something over 400,000, and I would say a later count would show that this total has now reached more than 500,000. But even at 400,000, the figure we were given a few days ago, why were not these public projects brought out, if they were real, in order to relieve that unemployment? Today many people are in desperate circumstances. I know that in several communities from which I have heard unemployment is so great that many people are almost facing starvation. Yet the government refrains from putting into effect this shelf of public works that were promised before the election. A short time ago I read an address by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) himself to the chamber of commerce of Montreal, I believe, in which he was reported as having said that the government was expecting and depending upon private enterprise to supply employment to the Canadian people.
He was further quoted as saying that the shelves of public works were not intended for that purpose, only under conditions and circumstances named by the government. So to all intents and purposes this was just a June 27 promise; and it did bring results. In all my memory, Mr. Speaker, going back over

many years in political life, I must say I do not think there was ever an administration that entertained such callous disregard for truth toefore an election and such utter contempt for promises made after an election as the government now surrounding the Prime Minister.
Let us look a little further at some of the government's election promises. Mine is an agricultural province, and as a member representing Prince Edward Island I take pride in the fact that nowhere in all Canada will you find more skilful or more scientific or more productive use made of the land than in that province. Nor have we stopped at farming the land alone. In our rich Malpeque oyster beds we even farm the bottom of the sea. I believe not only the maritime provinces but also the rest of Canada can take a lesson in farming and producing from the soil of that little province of Prince Edward Island.
This government promised our farmers markets for butt'er, cheese, eggs, poultry, bacon and potatoes, as well as other things. Last spring before the election, when there was a surplus of potatoes, the government purchased all the potatoes the farmers had in the bins at 69 cents per bushel. A farmer could then use those potatoes for feed purposes, or if he chose he could dump them on the compost heap. This created the impression, in fact the promise was made, that the government would see that the farmers were protected this year on the price of surplus potatoes. Have they done so? Not as yet, nor does the problem seem to be anywhere near settled. Delegation after delegation waits on the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), to see if some assistance can be secured.
Let me look at another government promise. Before the election of June 27, the aged people across Canada were promised old age pensions without a means test. Was that promise kept? No. Furthermore, to the men who were retired on small pensions, such as the men who had been working on the railway and were retired on an allowance of $27, $30, $40 or even $50 per month, the promise was held out that they would be able to secure the old age pension without a means test. Nothing has been done about implementing that promise, and it looks as if nothing will be done.
I should like to consider further this question of unemployment. Unemployment is growing everywhere, and it is becoming more difficult' all the time to keep it under control. Even in the small province from which I come, there is a great deal of unemployment. It has reached such proportions that the mayor of Charlottetown issued a proclamation to all citizens requesting their assistance
The Address-Mr. McLure in a jobs campaign, in an effort to overcome the growing number of unemployed who are daily seeking food and lodging. It is difficult to have to mention these things which are happening in your own constituency, but I am mentioning facts. If some of these promises had been fulfilled, especially those concerning public works, the city of Charlottetown would not have half the unemployment it has today.
Speaking about public works, I may say that the city of Charlottetown certainly needs public works. For the last three or four years, we have been promised a public building to house all the dominion offices and the post office. Although it has been promised for three years, it is difficult to get a statement about that public building. Even the site of it has not been fully established. The land owners and tenants, who have been ordered to vacate their premises by April 1, are wondering what the public works department is going to do. Many of these people have not had their properties appraised, nor have they been paid for them. I believe this is something that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) should attend to immediately. I hope he will not keep these things a secret. I should like to know how many of these land owners have had their properties appraised, whether they are going to be paid for them, or whether the government is going to walk in and take the land, then make a settlement afterwards. I believe this house, and the people of Prince Edward Island, should have a statement from the Minister of Public Works as to when construction of the building will be commenced. In the interests of solving the unemployment problem, construction should be begun immediately.
There are other matters with which I should like to deal. For instance, the city of Charlottetown has been promised harbour improvements for years. The Andrew Rae Duncan commission strongly recommended these harbour improvements. Perhaps the Minister of Public Works will say that certain improvements are being made. I will admit that some money has been voted for the last two or three years for improvement's to the shipping sheds on the marine and railway wharf. Apart from that, these promised harbour improvements have been dangled before us. One harbour improvement which would create a great deal of employment is the building of a marine railway slip. This was definitely promised by all parties as far back as 1911.
In 1911, the Conservative party promised to build a drydock, or marine railway slip as it is probably called now. When the Borden government came into power, it immediately started to fulfil its promises. The main one

The Address-Mr. McLure was the Borden-Tormentine ferry that was there promised and they fulfilled it, giving us the first real communication we had with the mainland, even if we had gone in under terms for proper transportation in 1873. Besides this, the Borden government went to work and purchased a shore property on which to build a marine railway slip, or, call it what you will, a place for making repairs to our steamers. What happened? They bought the property. They let the contract for the machinery to firms in Liverpool in England, but the war broke out and this matter was left dangling again until 1921 when it was again raised as a promise to the city of Charlottetown that a marine railway slip would be built.
There is the work there for a slip. We have our own boats that always have to be repaired. For instance, this railway slip should be built to take care of all the boats in the service for the province of Prince Edward Island; it should be built to accommodate all our ships. Here are a few of them that are in the government service: the Brant, the Sorel, the Prince Nova, the Charles A. Dunning, the Prince Edward Island, and the S.S. Ahegweit. In addition to these there are all the small ferry boats running between various points on the island, as well as the tugs and dredges. If we had a proper marine railway slip repairs to these boats would give employment to 200 or probably 250 men the year round right in the city of Charlottetown alone. We have the mechanics and the machine shops that can do all this work. But where does it go? Every particle of it is taken away from our province; as is said, we cannot work below the water line. Where does it go? It goes to Pictou, Halifax, Saint John and Sorel; thousands and thousands of dollars' worth of work is going away that should be available for the employment of our own labourers in the province of Prince Edward Island. In addition there is the danger entailed in taking these boats on the trip up to Sorel or even to Saint John or Halifax. In 1941 we lost the S.S. Charlottetown when she was on a trip up to Saint John, I think it was, for the purpose of overhaul. We should have from this government some assurance as to whether they are going to endeavour in any way to fulfil the promises made during the last election campaign and for years before that.
A little while ago I said it was difficult to get information on any subject dealing with matters in our province. From time to time I have had my difficulties with regard to particular matters concerning our own constituency. I want to cite one of them which

occurred here a few days ago. On March 6 I directed to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) a question which was as follows, as reported at page 467 of Hansard:
I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Transport. Has the Canadian National Railways made a general proposal to all the other provinces similar to that which has been made to the government of the province of Prince Edward Island, namely, to take over all the highway bus and truck services, and to place them under the control of the board of transport commissioners.
Here is the answer I received from the minister:
That is quite an order. I have had no advance notice of the question, but I may tell my hon. friend that I am not aware of any such movement. In any event I am sure that the Canadian National Railways, or for that matter the federal government, would have no jurisdiction over provincial highways on Prince Edward Island, and over one or two of the other matters which my hon. friend mentioned in his question. That is about the only information I can give him at this time.
The minister's answer was really a surprise to me when he stated that he was unaware of any such matters going on between the government of one province and the Canadian National Railways of the dominion. Surely the minister should be aware of what is taking place in connection with the Canadian National Railways transport matters. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I should now like to give him a little bit of information, as follows. Negotiations had been going on for a long time between the Canadian National Railways and the province of Prince Edward Island. As a matter of fact, the railways presented a brief; and in that brief they outlined all that they were willing to do and what they wanted to procure for themselves in this swap. We all know, of course, that the whole question would be one of jurisdiction unless it could be amicably agreed to between the parties. However, whatever the board of transport commissioners and the public utilities commission decided upon would be all that was required to have this highway traffic system established. The government of Prince Edward Island were so much at sea with regard to this railways' brief that was presented that they could not come to a conclusion. They did not feel like accepting, and neither did they feel like rejecting, the proposals of the Canadian National Railways for them to get co-ordination of the bus, truck and railway services all under the Canadian National Railways management in that province.
Before the railways' brief was presented, and it is dated February 15, a great deal had transpired by letter and conversation; because on February 22 the Prince Edward Island

government stated in a letter to the vicepresident and general manager of the Canadian National Railways at Moncton as follows:
Please accept for yourself and convey to Mr. F. A. Gaffney our appreciation for the lucid presentation of proposals contained in your letter of February 15, and for the exceedingly clear and forceful manner in which the same was presented verbally on February 8 and 9.
I have before me a clipping with reference to the whole matter giving the full details and the full brief of the Canadian National Railways. It is too long to read, but I shall be glad to send it over to the minister. Then I should like to have my question really answered, and the question is this.
Has the Canadian National Railways made a general proposal to all the other provinces similar to that which has been made to the government of the province of Prince Edward Island?
If they have, and if the governments of the different provinces were to accept it, the Canadian National Railways would be in absolute control of all transportation not only in and out of the province but in control of all transportation and the highways of the province. There must be something in it or they would not have gone to such detail in making up such a long brief.
I should now like to touch a little on transportation. To a province like Prince Edward Island, which is largely agricultural, transportation is without doubt the most important problem. I have endeavoured to emphasize that on the floor of the house several times since 1945. We have grappled with all the governments to see if we could not get the promises of confederation properly fulfilled. We have argued with them; we have tried different ways. So far we have had a certain amount of success. That success was accorded to us by the Borden government when they inaugurated the Borden-Tormentine ferry system.
For a few minutes I should like to give a little information regarding a second ferry system that we have in Prince Edward Island, and which has been in operation during the summer months, namely, the Northumberland ferry service from Wood Islands to Caribou, known as the Wood Islands-Caribou ferry service. Before the last war private enterprise took up this matter and established the ferry boats. At that time a great many people thought that private enterprise was making a mistake. Public works helped them build their docks for docking, and gave them some other assistance. The government also gave them a subsidy. That system has now grown to such an extent that the Canadian National Railways, and perhaps the government as
The Address-Mr. McLure well, are anxious to get control over it. The Northumberland ferry was first brought to the attention of the Canadian National Railways when they had to reduce their fares on the Borden ferry to compete with the Northumberland ferry. The idea is to get control, and it was rumoured for quite some time that that was what was going on. I asked a question with reference to it. There must have been something in the rumour. I could deal with it if I had a little more time.
When the Northumberland ferries were making their contract with the government they had written into the contract what the fare would be, and the farmers knew what they would have to pay for their produce being trucked across by this ferry.
Another part of Prince Edward Island which was promised a ferry, and which should have it, is the West Point-Buctouche area. This was one of the live issues during the last election campaign; but since then, like many others, it has been thrown into the discard. The farmers up there seem still anxious to have that ferry system.
As I said a moment ago, transportation to our province is the greatest problem, and the most important one that we have. I want to put on record the growth and development of the Wood Islands-Caribou ferry. It was stated when they started that they would not carry a thousand cars. Last year 67,000 passengers were carried from the first of May to the first of November, which is the period they run. During that time they carried 16,000 automobiles and over 5,000 commercial trucks. This will show hon. members why we have the rumours that the Canadian National Railways, or some governing body, want to get hold of this ferry, even if there is no railway line running to either terminal. It has already been said that if the government or the Canadian National Railways take over this ferry they will put on a boat that will be 50 per cent larger than the present largest boat there. That might be looked upon as quite a promise. Why do I say that?, I say that because the Charles A. Dunning, one of the larger boats that we have there, draws too much water at certain times. We had extreme difficulty in getting the Minister of Public Works to dredge the harbour further so that she could dock properly. There seems to be some underlying principle or motive in the whole thing, which is to get absolute control of our ferry system and of our transportation system on Prince Edward Island.

Will the minister advise, instruct and demand that the Canadian National Railways provide reefer cars for the shipment of potatoes and turnips from Prince Edward Island? The shortage of reefer cars at the present time is the greatest they have experienced1 in years.

I should like to deal with a question asked yesterday by the hon. member for Queens. It had to do with the supply of reefer cars and part of it was to this effect.

I promised the hon. member that I would get a report from the Canadian National Railways. I am advised by them today that there are 454 reefer cars on hand1 or in transit for Prince Edward Island traffic.
They might have been five thousand miles away and still have been in transit.
This total is made up as follows:
Cars on P.E.1	 292
In transit at Cape Tormentine	 43
Moncton	 30
Truro	 22
Campbellton	 22
Monk	 45
Total	 454
Officers of the Canadian National Railways report that a satisfactory position as to reefer cars is considered to be around 300. When it exceeds this figure there is danger of transportation difficulties arising in connection with the movement of the cars. Therefore my hon. friend can see that there is no shortage of cars. On the contrary, the situation is a good one.
May I say in closing that the onus was placed upon my shoulders when it was suggested that I had given wrong information and did not have the facts of the case. However, while at that time I did not reply, I knew I had the correct information, and really felt sorry that the minister had been so misinformed, or that he had received the wrong information from someone.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, allow me to congratulate you on the flawless way in which you carried out your high responsibilities throughout the second session of 1949. I also wish to congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and his colleagues on the choice they have made in selecting Mr. Larson and Mr. Dumas as mover and seconder of the address.
I also wish to take this opportunity to extend my congratulations to the hon. member for Kindersley, the mover of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, as well as to my good friend, the member for Ville-neuve, whose constituency is next to mine. He brought out all the most interesting and important points concerning his county and northern Quebec. He certainly deserved the honour which has fallen to him. I am also extremely pleased to congratulate him on having been elected with such an overwhelming majority as the representative of this new and beautiful county of Villeneuve which so proudly bears the name of the illustrious late prelate. The Liberal party is fortunate in having men of his stamp, who work for the development of our beautiful country.
Mr. Speaker, I now wish to deal with a subject very dear to my heart, namely the county of Chapleau, which I have the honour to represent and which is one of Canada's wealthiest districts as far as agriculture, mining and lumbering industries are concerned. In connection with agriculture, I pointed out in my first speech in this house, in 1945, that in 1944 we had harvested, in the Abitibi district, $25,150 worth of wheat, $472,540 worth of oats, $31,680 worth of barley and $2,261,500 55946-46!
The Address-Mr. D. Gourd worth of hay, not to mention thousands of dollars worth of buckwheat, rye, peas, beans and mixed grain. Moreover, our potato crop amounted to $587,820, which does not include the returns from alfalfa, turnips and corn. For that reason, I beg the Department of Agriculture to assist as much as possible this new part of the country through grants for cold storage and drainage. The Kapuskasing experimental farm being quite remote, the district should have enough agronomists to establish demonstration farms in every parish. Needless to say, a promoter specially attached to our district would be quite welcome.
I also emphasized, in another speech I made in 1946, the importance of the mines located in the northern part of the province of Quebec and I mentioned the mining of such metals as gold, copper, etc. Here are the figures I gave:	the yield in gold was $32
million, and in copper, $22 million, these amounts being exclusive of all other minerals. I then added that in the best interests of our national economy, the government should continue providing assistance to mines.
During the same speech I also said that we had exported 100 million feet of cord wood as well as millions of cords of pulpwood. Since there are such abundant natural resources in my constituency, they should be developed. First, the railroad between Barraute and Beattyville, which follows exactly the same gold mining zone and so forth, should be extended to Bachelor lake and later to Chi-bougamou. At present, several mining companies cannot work their mines due to a lack of transport facilities. I therefore appeal more particularly to the Canadian National Railways to examine further all the requests sent me by public bodies, such as municipalities, chambers of commerce and the economic planning council, which all show the urgent need for building this railroad immediately. As I already said in a speech I made in 1949, would it not be fair that Quebec should secure from the federal government the funds required to build, within the province, a section of the trans-Canada highway proportionate to those in other provinces? I said that the present highway, leaving the Manitoba boundary at 35 miles from Kenora and passing through Fort William, Kapuskasing and Ottawa, is 1,390 miles long. I would also point out that the highway from Point Fortune in the province of Quebec to the New Brunswick boundary, near Edmundston, covers a

The Address-Mr. D. Gourd distance of 388 miles. That means that it is located in Ontario to the extent of 75 per cent. If my proposal were carried out, the road starting at Kenora would still pass through Fort William, Hearst, Kapuskasing and Cochrane. It would cover a distance of 894 miles in Ontario. From Cochrane, it would head for La Reine in the province of Quebec and thence through La Sarre, Mont Laurier, Montreal and so on until it reached the New Brunswick boundary. The highway would then cover a distance of 828 miles in the province of Quebec, which would seem fair to both provinces. This alternative would also make the distance from the western provinces and northern Ontario to Ottawa, Montreal and Quebec 56 miles shorter. I do not see why the Ontario government does not build a road over the mere forty miles between Norembega and La Reine. This has been long requested by the boards of trade, and I know whereof I speak because I have been chairman of the Amos board of trade.
A short while ago, I organized a delegation of some of my constituents to meet northern Ontario boards of trade, M.P.'s and M.P.P.'s and get them to keep on exerting pressure on the government of Ontario and urge it to carry this road as far as the Quebec boundary, at La Reine. This connection means a great deal to us all, for it would help strengthen the ties of good will between the two provinces. '
To these suggestions, may I be permitted to add another very important one. It is about unemployment. We feel it a little, as everyone knows. Would it not be possible to reach an agreement with the government of Quebec to help colonization by building new roads to the north, as far as lake Mistassini and Mattagami? In addition, this would be a good way to check unemployment. Colonization would be the first to profit by the roads that would lead towards new land and I am sure that with the assistance given to settlers by the Quebec government, the unemployed in question would all take advantage of such developments to go and settle in these parts.
If I have spoken of my constituency and of its natural wealth as represented by agriculture, mines and forests, and if moreover I have taken the liberty of requesting your aid in developing it, it is because I earnestly wish for the progress of my constituency, that is to say, for that of my own country.
