speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to join those who have preceded me in this debate and congratulate the mover (Mr. Larson) and the seconder (Mr. Dumas). Their constituents must feel justly proud of their representatives in this house. I do not propose to tell the house all about the constituency which I have the honour to represent as that would take too long. However, I do intend to present to hon. members an idea which, if it turns out to be sound, as some of us think it is, will help to solve the present unsatisfactory economic condition of the maritimes. I believe this is the first time this project has been discussed in public.
In my opinion the maritime provinces are the best place in the world to live in, but we lack some of the economic advantages enjoyed by other parts of Canada. We complain because we have not enough industry and were not allotted enough industry during the war. The reason has always been given that we have not enough power. We have plenty of coal but not enough electricity. I am sure that everyone in this house is willing to help the maritimes and we have been told many times to present our problem and we would have all the assistance we needed in arriving at a solution.
I believe the solution has been found. It is called the, St. Mary's tidal project which it is claimed will develop a maximum of 2,336,250 horsepower. This development would take place in the counties of Westmorland and Albert in New Brunswick, and Cumberland in Nova Scotia. I should like to take this opportunity to pay my respects to the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black), who returned to the house this afternoon, and to wish him the best of health for the remainder of the session.
If this project were completed the Chignecto canal could not be built over the proposed route for reasons which I shall give later. I do not wish it to appear that I am trying to prevent the building of the Chignecto canal and the development of hydroelectric power at that site; I am suggesting an alternative plan which would provide for a canal and the development of two and a third million horsepower as compared with the 135,000 horsepower that would be developed under the proposed Chignecto plan. If this plan is adopted much credit will go to the Chignecto canal committee which has done so much to mould public opinion into realizing the need for some such plan.
The St. Mary's tidal project is the brain child of Mr. W. A. S. Melanson, C.E., M.E.I.C.,

of Moncton, New Brunswick, and is the result of many long years of study and work. He is to be congratulated upon his vision. Not every possible site for tidal power development has been investigated, and the remarks which follow will deserve the attention of all persons interested in the welfare of the mari-times. The study of any tidal power development in the maritimes could not be justly undertaken without reference to and a review of the report on tidal power, Petitcodiac and Memramcook estuaries, as published by the department of mines and resources, Canada, 1945, part 1-test, and part 2-plans, disclosing full results and findings of the field investigations carried out from August, 1944, to October, 1945, by the firm of H. G. Acres and Company, consulting engineers, Niagara Falls, Ontario.
Unfortunately the adverse findings of this report from an economical standpoint have prejudiced public opinion to such a degree that too few have bothered to read it in full. It is doubtful if our men of letters or science, either within or without our institutions of higher learning, have given this all-important subject of maritime welfare the study it most assuredly deserves. Notwithstanding this seeming prejudice, this report contains concise, terse treatises on tides peculiar to the bay of Fundy and its tributaries; on the astronomical effects of the moon and sun in their various phases on the tides; on rock-fill dam construction on unstable foundations; on inlet and outlet gate structures; on various types of hydraulic turbines and their selection; on electric generators with power house and transformer station design. All these subjects, with many others, are interwoven into a mass of finite scientific information, permitting a proper step by step design of each and every structure embodied in such a large development.
The economic feasibility of the entire project was defeated by two adverse physical features of the site. These were, first, the existence of 80 feet of silt, mud and gravel in the beds of both estuaries; second, the great difference in the relative size of the two estuaries. I will not go farther into the reasons why the Petitcodiac tidal project was unsound, except to say that if it could have been built on a more favourable site a saving of nearly half the estimated cost could have been made.
Situated ten miles from the Petitcodiac-Memramcook estuaries, there exists the confluence of the Shepody bay and Cumberland basin at the head of Chignecto bay. These two relatively large estuaries are separated by the rock-bound Maringouin peninsula that terminates in a low headland at cape Maringouin, which juts out westerly a distance of
The Address-Mr. George one mile into Shepody bay. Here Shepody bay, with its tributaries covering an area of 70 square miles, and Cumberland basin, with its tributaries covering an area of 60 square miles, are separated by the narrow cape Maringouin. It is proposed to construct two barriers, one from the westerly side of cape Maringouin across Shepody bay to join with the rock masses of Grindstone island and St. Mary's point, and the other from the easterly side of cape Maringouin to Ragged point on the Nova Scotia shore.
Of the many physical features of the existing rock masses that would enter into the general scheme of this proposal, the greatest and most advantageous is the present rock formation of St. Mary's point. Jutting out from the mainland at Harvey bank, Albert county, there is a peninsula of rock formation that extends in an easterly direction to St. Mary's point. It then crosses St. Mary's ledge, St. Mary's anchorage, Grindstone ledge and Grindstone island, the outer tip of which was at one time the original St. Mary's point. The height or elevation of the St. Mary's and Grindstone ledges are just below mean sea level and therefore would permit the economic construction of a large number of inlet gates. St. Mary's anchorage or Grindstone island would be ideal for the construction of a navigation lock to permit ship passage at all times. The length of the St. Mary's peninsula is 3 miles, a little over half the distance across the mouth of Shepody bay. These facts explain the origin of the title given to this proposed tidal power. The outlet gates, power house and additional inlet gates would be located at or near the south end of the Maringouin peninsula, a very central location for the distribution of power to the entire maritime provinces.
British admiralty chart No. 354 indicates the existence of the rock formation in the bed of Shepody bay at an average depth of eight fathoms below chart datum, while across the upper portion of Chignecto bay the rock formation is indicated at an average depth of five fathoms below chart datum. Very little mud or silt is indicated except on the south side of Maringouin peninsula, where there exists a body of mud. However, this is a decided asset as it will be required to make the core of the Cumberland basin dam. Mud for the Shepody barrier can be obtained from the Shepody or New Horton flats. Therefore, drilling and testing for foundations are not necessary, as not one iota of doubt exists about the rock formations.
The question of choosing either the Cumberland or the Shepody basin for the high and

The Address-Mr. George low water basins has been given careful consideration from all economical and practical angles. These are as follows:
1.	The rock formation across the mouth of the Cumberland basin is just at the proper elevation for the most economical construction of outlet gates.
2.	The southeast side of the Maringouin peninsula is the only practical location for the power house.
3.	A rock-fill dam with mud core is the only economical manner of erecting a barrier across the mouth of Shepody bay.
4.	The head channel can be cheaply excavated across cape Maringouin and rock used in the rock-fill dam across Shepody bay and part of Cumberland basin and permit construction of a series of inlet gates near the power house.
5.	The St. Mary's rock formation permits very economical construction of inlet gates, of which there must be a large number.
6.	Along the shores of Cumberland basin and its tributaries there exists the bulk of the marshlands in the maritimes, estimated to contain 40,000 acres. Using Cumberland as a low level basin will reclaim all marshlands and will forever do away with the necessity for dikes and aboiteaux. It will thereby save the federal government, the provincial government and the farmers the high cost of reclamation.
7.	The existence of a large gypsum processing plant at Hillsborough, working twenty-four hours a day, with United States markets, depends in large part on water transportation for their supplies to reach the market. Also the proposed construction of a fertilizer plant at Weldon will require water transportation.
8.	Of the two basins, Shepody bay is recognized as the one taking precedence in volume of navigation.
Shepody bay has therefore been proposed as the head basin and the Cumberland basin as the low water basin. The designation of the Cumberland basin as the low water basin for economic reasons will somewhat alter the proposed scheme of a canal across the isthmus. However, this proposed power development is so vast and will be so beneficial to the entire maritimes that the greatest benefit to the greatest number must be our guiding spirit.
Much praise and credit is due to the Chig-necto canal committee, to the group of businessmen and to the newspapers that so nobly supported them in their struggle to make the maritimes and Canada conscious of the necessity of the navigation canal. Mr. R. Herbert Cooper, who saw the possibilities of the development of power along with the canal benefits, is deserving of much praise. His

scheme is practical and contains much merit. The use of Cumberland basin as a tail race basin in a big tidal power development will not diminish the necessity for a Chignecto canal; it will rather enhance its cause.
Out of the Shepody basin there are two or three possible routes. All proposed routes have merits and some demerits, but ultimately would join the waters of the Petitcodiac river with Shediac harbour. There is one route that possesses many natural features. Along this route the distance from Moncton harbour to Shediac harbour is 15 miles. This route would reduce the distance between the bay of Fundy points and upper Canada by approximately 75 miles over the proposed route across the Chignecto isthmus.
The tidal factors which make the development of power possible are long and detailed. I will not go into them. I have here the data on Fundy tides and the possible power development; and with the permission of the house I should like to place it on Hansard.

From the information available, it would appear that Mr. Melanson's project is workable. It is estimated that the cost will be in the vicinity of $190 per commercial horsepower. This compares favourably with present-day construction, which is from $200 to $250 per horsepower. I do not feel that the capital cost is as important as the operating cost. If the operating costs and, upkeep are nominal, and we can get this vast supply of cheap power, then the expenditure would be justified.
The federal government is spending large sums of money protecting approximately
40,000	acres of marshland from the sea. The building of this project would protect the lands in the Cumberland basin area, and would save several millions of dollars which are required to reclaim these lands. There would be no more maintenance on dikes and aboiteaux.
In the Petitcodiac river area the water level might be above the marshlands. In this case, I am told on good authority that there would be no problem in draining the land by the use of pumps as in Holland. There should be sufficient cheap power available for that purpose. The other alternative would be to buy the land and let it out to sea.

I have great faith in the future of the maritimes. We are gradually turning from a wood economy to an agricultural economy. The forests have been depleted faster than reforestation has taken place. We are building for the future, and in a hundred years the world will need all the food it can produce. In order to prosper in the maritimes we must have industry, and industry must have an abundance of cheap power; I am sure there would be a ready sale for all that can be produced. I sincerely hope that the government will see its way clear to start a survey of this project immediately. I might suggest two phases of this study. First, a review of the H. G. Acres report, as applied to the St. Mary's idea; second, an actual engineering report on the St. Mary's project.
Another good reason, Mr. Speaker, for doing something about the project appears in a press release in the Moncton Daily Times, under date of March 10, 1950. It is headed, "Opposed to Quoddy bill," and reads as follows:
The budget bureau informed congress today President Truman opposes a pending bill to establish the Passamaquoddy tidal-power project.
If we needed any more reason, Mr. Speaker, I think we have it right there.
I am not asking for this because it is a part of our maritime rights. I feel that we have heard too much about that. I ask for it because we are part of Canada, and because all our natural resources should be developed in order that we may continue to play our part in contributing to the prosperity of the dominion.

speechtext:
Like most hon. members who spoke before me, I am pleased to congratulate the mover of the address to His Excellency the Governor General, the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Larson) and the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Dumas), the seconder, for the manner in which both fulfilled their task.
I also take this opportunity to congratulate Mr. Speaker-who is not here right now-and his assistants who have presided with fairness over the debates. I also wish to congratulate my colleagues for their courtesy to the members of the opposition, and for being so kind to them although I feel sometimes they are .much given to exaggeration. However, I do not envy their fate for there is every indication that the Liberal party will be in office for many years.
Divine Providence protects us by giving us men as talented as our Prime Minister, the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent.
I thank the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner)-who I am happy to see at his
The Address-Mr. J. O. Gour desk-and all the members of the cabinet for the support prices on agricultural products such as bacon, butter, cheese, eggs and so forth.
I have the honour of representing a constituency both urban and rural in character. I know that in Russell, thousands of farmers are very thankful to the government for this help. Several farmers of my constituency own herds of more than fifty milk cows, market each year from 200 to 300 hogs, and keep flocks numbering 7,000 to 8,000 hens, which they raise for the sale of eggs and poultry.
The dairy cattle of our county have been tuberculin tested for more than twenty years. Last year, my constituency obtained the best results in Ontario. As a result our cattle find a large number of purchasers, especially in the United States; this enables our farmers to breed cattle on a large scale and get satisfactory prices for their herds. They are less concerned with the high price of their products than with their net earnings with which they are supposed to live decently on the farm.
Like myself, farmers feel that the price of what they buy is too high. That also goes for the cost of living for our urban population, particularly of the workers.
I have the honour of including in my constituency one of the most prosperous towns in Canada. I refer to Eastview where an extremely up-to-date high school, a community centre, a hospital and other buildings indicative of its increasing importance are now seen beside other great institutions.
My riding includes many other localities of note, for instance Manor Park, an attractive village which is but three years old; Rockcliffe, where the most important airport for national defence is located; Overbrook and Billings Bridge, blessed by the fact that the diocesan seminary is built in the vicinity; Billings Bridge, moreover, connects with Uplands, one of the most important points for commercial air transportation. Finally, there are many other small towns inhabited by wage earners all of whom agree in hoping for a lower cost of living.
In my opinion manufacturers should be content with a smaller profit and undertake to compete on world markets. I think their profits are inordinately large and their prices too high. Farm implements, motorcars,
720	HOUSE OF COMMONS
The Address-Mr. J. O. Gour
ranges, refrigerators, furniture, textiles, lumber, plumbing and shoes are all too dear by 10 to 20 per cent.
If they cut down their prices, manufacturers would increase sales and enable farmers and small wage earners a better chance to buy more of those goods. This would compel them to increase production, which would entail an increase in manpower and would thus stem unemployment.
I can hear hon. members opposite deplore the loss of our markets and the ridiculous prices obtained for our produce. Let me remind them, however, of the years of 1930 to 1935, when our farmers were selling 200 pound hogs for $7 to $8, shipping prepaid, cattle weighing from 1,000 to 1,200 pounds for $12 to $15, shipping also prepaid, while the present government pays a premium or subsidy of $8 on a two hundred pound hog, grade A select, for export, which now brings the farmer from $40 to $50. An animal weighing from 1,000 to 1,200 pounds now sells for $125 to $150, that is ten times more than in 1942.
If I am not mistaken, one or two local agreements are made by two or more persons, while international agreements are made by two or more governments. Here, therefore, is the first rule. It is the price that counts. We have proof of that. We gave billions to Great Britain. I voted in favour of that bill myself; we did more than anybody in the world to help other nations out of their predicaments and we are still willing to do so. When the time comes to arrive at an agreement, the only thing that counts is the price of the goods. After all, that is only natural; that is the human way of looking at things!
All agree that we are one of the most skilful nations; then we can produce so as to meet the prices of the other honest competitors without lowering our present standard of living.
I would point out that people should spend less money on alcoholic beverages because, first, alcohol degrades the soul and too often takes up a considerable part of the essential income of large families. The same thing applies to many forms of entertainment which are far from being necessary to the welfare of our people.
Mr. Speaker, I believe I have given a suggestion which could prevent unemployment;
I now wish to suggest another way of going about it. Since the government of the beautiful province of Ontario, in which 1 live,

does nothing to help the farmers I feel compelled to request more from the federal government. I would therefore request the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott)-he is not here but I trust that he will read my speech, which I have already mentioned to him-as well as the Minister of Agriculture to improve farm loans. Let me give an example. A hundred acre farm with good buildings warrants a loan of about $4,000. How can a farmer set up his sons or how can a young man try to set himself up on a farm with such a small amount? First, it costs about $4,000 to get an average herd of cattle and the equipment necessary to operate this farm, not considering the $10,000 to $12,000 required for the farm itself. If this farmhouse were built in a city, a loan of $4,000 or more could easily be secured. I therefore maintain and assert that the farm loan is not practical for our farmers.
More than half the farmers of my district did not apply because they feel it is useless. According to information I have from reliable sources, approximately half of the applications for farm loans were turned down during 1949-50 in Ontario.
I have also a request to make to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) and to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier). I have here a plan in connection with the Nation river project, and works already carried out by the Ontario government. I am pleased to congratulate our provincial government for this well-balanced plan. I could submit a copy to each of the ministers concerned. I would now like to read a few lines showing clearly the importance of this plan. I would then ask the house that it be put on record.
(Text):
The south Nation watershed is an area of 1,511 square miles in the extreme easterly part of Ontario, and includes parts of the counties of Prescott, Russell, Dundas, Stormont, Glengarry, Carleton and Grenville.
From southwest to northeast, the watershed extends about 76 miles in a direct line, and its greatest width, from northwest to southeast, is about 35 miles. From the source of the area of the main river to its mouth is a distance of 69 miles, in a direct line.
There are no cities or large towns on the watershed; but there are a number of incorporated villages, including Winchester, with a population of 1,094; Chesterville, 1,241; Casselman, 1,089; Finch, 390; and Maxville, 812. In addition there are a few villages, which have not been incorporated, the largest of which are as follows: Spencerville, South Mountain, Crysler, Metcalfe, Moose Creek, Limoges, Russell and Bourget.
From the above, it will be seen that the watershed, by and large, is essentially a rural area of Ontario.

(Translation):
This plan consists in carrying out excavation and damming, which are most urgent and necessary since they would be extremely useful to the people who live in a dozen municipalities: Matilda, Mounta, Winchester, Edwardsburg, Augusta, Finch, Cambridge, Plantagenet South, Alfred, Plantagenet North, Chesterville and Casselman. I will read another passage from the same plan, with special reference to the damaged parts.
(Text):
Floods on the south Nation watershed present a serious threat to the livelihood of the people in all the municipalities in the area, and are detrimental to the economy of all neighbouring business centres. Indeed, it is self-evident that the periodic destruction of crops, the washing out of roads and bridges and the carrying away of thousands of tons of the best top soil in any area represents an important loss to the whole province.
Unfortunately, these severe losses are not rare phenomena but, on the contrary, have occurred in twenty-six out of the thirty years in the period1 1918 to 1947 inclusive. And in six of these years the Nation river overflowed its banks at least twice in the same year.
The severity of these inundations is increasing, as is attested by the 1938 and 1947 floods which were the greatest on record.
The most extensive flooding occurs in two areas: the Brinston flooded area located above Chesterville and comprising fertile lands in Winchester, Matilda and Mountain townships and the Cobb lake area, including the flats adjacent to the river from Lemieux to Plantagenet Springs.
The flood of 1938 inundated an area at Brinston of approximately 24 square miles to a maximum depth of 9 feet.
Many dwellings had two to three feet of water over their ground floors. The 1947 flood is reported to have been just about as severe.
Floods during spring freshets cause inconvenience, hardship and distress. Farmers do what they can to meet the threat: livestock and supplies are moved to upper floors or other safe locations and seeding is delayed until the spring floods are past. The duration of these floods from the time of overtopping the bank to the recession below the banks has lasted for as long as nine and one-half days.
These floods are not confined to the spring freshets but have frequently occurred after heavy summer storms. In fact, these are the most damaging as crops are either washed out completely or ruined through lying under water. It is reported that at least one farmer lost crops four years in succession through flooding.
I shall not read all this brief because I do not want to weary hon. members, but I should like to have it included in Hansard. I think the minister concerned should have a copy of it.
(Translation):
The project is not very costly, slightly over $2 million, and should be shared by the provincial and dominion governments. Because it will be undertaken in rural centres, municipalities are not in a position of paying any
The Address-Mr. J. O. Gour share of it. It should be remembered that elsewhere in Canada irrigation projects are financed by federal and provincial authorities. The project would prevent the flooding of thousands of acres of good arable land, as well as supplying work in urban centres, which would alleviate unemployment.
I congratulate the government for passing a reforestation act last fall. Russell has the most important nursery in Canada, the "Larose Forest". Started over 20 years ago, it covers an area of more than 15,000 acres, comprising over 6 million trees: pine, fir, spruce, maple and so forth. We intend to increase it to at least 25 million trees. That is the reason I am requesting federal aid. I practise reforestation myself, having had trees planted on my own farms.
(Text):
On my own farm I have over 200,000 trees consisting of pine, spruce, maple and so forth. It gives me great pleasure to offer each hon. member of this house and of the other place, all newspapermen and all employees of the house, a tree for next Christmas free, on condition that they pay the transportation costs.
I take this opportunity to invite everyone who would like to see that forest next' May to let me know and it will give me great pleasure to accompany all hon. gentlemen who would like to go there to see it. If they do, they will see that we are doing our utmost to conserve the soil.
(Translation):
Flax is also grown on a large scale in the county of Russell. As I have the honour of being chairman of the national flax council, I take this opportunity of thanking the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) for what he has already done to help this industry. At the same time, I wish to ask him as well as the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) to grant us the financial assistance needed for the improvement of this industry already operating in Plessisville, in the beautiful province of Quebec, where flax is carded, spun and woven. Here is a sample of the work done in Plessisville. I am happy to show it to all the members of the house.
(Text):
This is what we call flax linen. This is a flax linen done with a cheaper grade of flax, what we call tow. This is a long fibre flax and it is manufactured in my own town of Casselman. This is the work we are doing with the flax fibre that I have here. Depending on the weather, and in good soil, this fibre grows up to from 36 to 44 inches long.

The Address-Mr. J. O. Gour (Translation):
I am in a position to show the benefits this development would mean for Canada.
If we had the factories needed to process this raw material, and to manufacture both thread and tow, at least in sufficient quantity to supply the home market, it would replace cotton and all other fibres of even less value which we have to import. This is the only fibre that can be grown in Canada and also the best in the world. At the present time we have to export 90 per cent of our raw material, both fibre and tow; we sell it at ridiculous prices and re-import it as linen, thread, etc., at exorbitant prices, often 20 to 30 times higher than we sold it. Such factories would also mean jobs for our workers and give farmers the opportunity to produce more flax. They could thus earn more money, to keep their sons on the farm, to hire workers who would help them grow this product because in order to supply only the needs of the country, we would require 400,000 to
500,000	acres of fibre flax.
An area of 1,000 acres sown with fibre flax gives jobs to 40 men, for six months, in our local factories, where flax undergoes a first treatment to extract the fibre and the seeds. This work is done from autumn to spring. This enables farmers' sons and local workers to find work during slack periods in rural centres. In my locality, we give employment to a great many men who would be without a job this winter.
The reason why I would like to get financial aid from the federal government and why I insist upon such help is that flax is produced in several provinces. I would like to see flax grown in every province, since flax gives good crops in fertile soil.
(Text):
Certified No. 1; germination, 96; variety, dominion. This group of farmers is a co-operative. I was for many years chairman and manager, but ceased my operations as manager when I was elected to the House of Commons. It was one of the finest ridings in Canada.
(Translation):
Everything in this plant in useful, seed grain, linseed-producing grain, fibres of all qualities which are used in all sorts of products, from shoemaker's thread to fishing lines, nets, etc. Waste products are used for poultry beddings, and several factories use it to provide power. That is what we do in Casselman
Linen, really the most important of these products, is very long wearing and is used for tablecloths, bedsheets, pillow slips, towels, underwear, dresses, etc.
(Text):
Cheaper fibres could be used today to manufacture overalls.
(Translation):
The cheaper linen, that of coarser fibre, is used for overalls, tarpaulins, tents, mail-bags, binder twine, etc.
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the government on having had a law passed during the last session abolishing appeals to the privy council, thus making the Supreme Court of Canada our final court of appeal. I believe our jurists are perfectly qualified. It was high time that this law was amended in a country such as ours.
I was also extremely gratified that another law was passed during the last session, enabling us to change our constitution without asking another country's permission.
I was also pleased to be a spectator at the federal-provincial conference, last January. I congratulate the right hon. Prime Minister on the very able fashion in which he presided over these meetings. I also would like to congratulate the various provincial premiers on the impartiality of their deliberations. I am convinced that subsequent conferences should follow the same pattern so that we would be able to amend our constitution in accordance with the requirements of our country's development, without infringing upon the legitimate rights of the provinces.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, may I state that it is high time for our country to have a distinctive flag, and by "distinctive" I mean a truly national flag bearing no trace of the emblems of the lands of our ancestors: France, England, Ireland or Scotland. Let us fcrget about the fleur-de-lis or the union jack. We are a nation and we need a flag. I have a model here which I believe would meet with the approval of all Canadians, and would help national unity and would thus increase national pride.
I also think that it would be appropriate for us to have a diplomatic representative at the Holy See; nearly all countries have one except the communist-controlled countries. I am convinced that this would have great diplomatic value for Canada. I wish that all the hon. members of this house would support this, for it should not be a matter of religion but really a diplomatic matter.

I also think that we should have a Canadian as the representative of His Majesty the King; we have Canadians as lieutenant governors of the provinces and there is no cause for complaint in this regard.
As a last request, Mr. Speaker, I believe we should allow the public to enter the galleries before we recite our beautiful opening prayer.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise for the first time in the house to speak on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. May I first of all join with those hon. members who have spoken before me in congratulating the mover (Mr. Larson) and the seconder (Mr. Dumas) of the address. They have done a good job and have indicated what legislation is likely to foe brought up for discussion. They have made suggestions which will be discussed thoroughly by hon. members.
May I congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) upon the appointment of the Hon. Elphege Marier, former member for Jacques Cartier, to the position of judge of the superior court of the district of Montreal. Mr. Marier, with his knowledge of law and the experience he has acquired through many years of practice, together with his sound judgment, qualities of heart and spirit of justice, is an ideal candidate to carry out the duties of judge. I congratulate Mr. Marier upon his appointment, which was well deserved. I am convinced that Mr. Marier will discharge his duties honourably and in conformity with the traditions of honesty known to exist in our courts of justice. This appointment created a vacancy which opened a door to my candidature and election as a member of this house.
Before going further let me introduce myself to the members of this house. I have the honour to represent the county which bears the name of the discoverer of Canada, Jacques Cartier. There are 36,000 electors in this county which comprises an agricultural section and a more important industrial section. Here we have the most important factories of Canada which have done so much with their skilled labour to help win the war and are continuing to help make Canada stronger and more prosperous, the Dominion Bridge Company, Dominion Engineering Works, two wire rope factories, a subsidiary of the Steel Company of Canada, Canadian Allis Chalmers, Jenkins Valves, all steel industries and many other smaller plants. These industries are prosperous and are still expanding.
In our midst we have an important distillery, Distillers Corporation. We also have an agricultural college, Macdonald college at
The Address-Mr. Leduc Ste. Anne de Bellevue. You will realize that I have the honour to represent a very important county.
I would like to have the experience and ability of some of the members of this house to discharge my duties as the representative of such an important county but I can assure the house that my desire to work and my devotion to the service of my constituents will supplement my oratorical ability.
We have a mixed population, about 35 per cent English-speaking and 65 per cent Frenchspeaking. The understanding and harmony between the two races have been very good. The understanding between the heads of the industries and the labour unions has been such that no walkouts or strikes have occurred for a number of years. Grievances have been worked out to mutual advantage, and our municipalities within the county have gone ahead and are prospering.
Being a new member, I do not intend at the beginning of this session to dictate my views to this house, but I am prepared to listen, study, gather experience and submit recommendations as the occasion arises.
May I be permitted to say that I intend to pursue the course of action which I have followed in supporting the Liberal party in measures that I consider the best under prevailing circumstances, reserving my liberty of action on matters being brought up which I would consider contrary to my principles and conscience, but I hope that such controversial matters will not occur during my term of office.
During the last two months I have been in this parliament I have had fairly good understanding with the ministers of the crown, although I am just an Independent Liberal. May I hope that full recognition will be made of my status in consideration of my past services to the Liberal party as organizer for 27 years without interruption of party affiliation, until I was called Independent. I supported the Prime Minister and I congratulate him upon his success in the general election, and I rejoice personally in the results I obtained on October 24.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Tomorrow being government day we will move to go into supply.
If the motion carries we will call three departments, transport, finance and fisheries. From eight to nine will be private and public bills. If there is a discussion on the motion to go into supply and we finish it some time during the day we will then take up the motion of the Secretary of State for External Affairs to refer his estimates to the external affairs committee. If we get through with that, we will take up the motion of the Minister of National Health and Welfare for the setting up of a committee on old age security.
That is one way of proceeding. If there is no debate on the motion to go into supply we will take up the estimates of transport.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: So that we may understand what the procedure will be, may I ask if it is the intention in the following weeks to call one department as was mentioned earlier?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Yes. I was not successful last week in getting the motion to go into supply agreed to by the house and could not call any departments. I find myself now with only the estimates of national defence that could be brought up on Friday. I hope to have them up on that day. I am asking for these three departments so that I shall have at least a few on which I can rely.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: I only asked the question for the purpose of understanding the situation. I thought when the suggestion was made that three departments would be called that that was carrying forward the original intention to call two departments last week and one this week. All I wanted to know was whether the course then would be followed of not calling more than one department each week hereafter.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: It is not the intention of the government to call more than one department unless there is some understanding as to the necessity of calling more than one.
At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
